title: GOP Rep. Hill says he'll weigh whether Hegseth's actions merit impeachment
summary: GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas was noncommittal about whether he would support an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Washington — GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas was noncommittal on Sunday about whether he would support an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as lawmakers are poised to return to Capitol Hill this week for the first time since voters delivered widespread rebuke in the midterm elections of the GOP — and the war in Iran.

"I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War," Hill said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Hegseth is expected to be under the microscope this week as long-brewing anger has come to the fore following the midterm elections, where Republicans saw brutal losses as many voters cited concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living. Before lawmakers left town for the campaign trail, outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth. This week, Massie said he plans to push ahead with forcing the vote.

Hill acknowledged that he's not satisfied with how the war has been handled. And he added that, "The commander in chief has to take the responsibility for the strategy of conducting the war and how it's been conducted."
"But I'll tell you one thing: There's nobody in America that wants Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Hill said. "This has been a goal of the United States for five decades."
Asked whether Hegseth should be impeached, Hill said, "The question is for the president: Should he continue to serve as the Secretary of War."
Hill also drew a distinction between Hegseth's job performance and whether he's committed impeachable offenses. Under the Constitution, the basis for impeachment is "high Crimes and Misdemeanors."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
The Arkansas Republican said that if Hegseth isn't "conducting his mission in the right way," then "then the president ought to make a change there."
"The question is: Are we leading at the Pentagon in the right way or not the right way?" Hill said. "That's very separate from whether or not somebody's committed an impeachable offense."

title: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
summary: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and former Robert F. Kennedy health adviser Calley Means join Margaret Brennan.
story: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts Rep. French Hill, Republican of Arkansas Calley Means, former White House senior adviser and top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, retired Navy vice admiral
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts
Rep. French Hill, Republican of Arkansas
Calley Means, former White House senior adviser and top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, retired Navy vice admiral
Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.

And this week on Face the Nation: In the aftermath of Tuesday's blue tsunami, Republicans regroup, President Trump makes a major staff change at the White House, and Democrats now face daunting challenges when it comes to getting stuff done.

Last week's decisive repudiation of the Trump agenda now puts Democrats on the spot. The pressure is on them to fix what voters say is wrong with the country. And that Democratic to-do list is a daunting one.
(Begin VT)
JOCELYN BENSON (D-Michigan Governor-Elect): Let's lower costs. Let's raise our wages. Let's end corruption.
SHERROD BROWN (D-Ohio Senator-Elect): We will fight to end these tariffs. We will end this war.
(CHEERING)
REP. CHRIS PAPPAS (D-NH) (Senator-Elect): It's expanding access to health care and childcare, saving Social Security.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Democrats may have won a healthy majority on Capitol Hill, but not a veto-proof margin. Can the two branches of government actually work together?
(Begin VT)
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): I will get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive. But I have to power of the veto.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will talk with two key players about the potential of bipartisanship when it comes to banking and financial legislation, Massachusetts Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Arkansas Congressman Republican French Hill.
At the White House, the finger-pointing over what led to the devastating defeat for the GOP intensifies, as Susie Wiles departs and Stephen Miller becomes the president's powerful chief of staff.

We talked with former White House health policy adviser Calley Means, who's gone public with damning accusations against Wiles and other top White House aides, saying they put special interests ahead of the MAHA agenda before the midterm elections. Did Means' allegations lead to Wiles' ouster?
(Begin VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Was it your intention to get her removed?
CALLEY MEANS (Former White House Senior Adviser): Yes.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.

Voters on Tuesday were loud and clear. They want action when it comes to high prices, and they want it now. How will the president handle working with the legislative branch to get that action Americans are demanding?
We will hopefully get some insights tonight, when 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat's interview with President Trump, which was taped Friday just before news of Susie Wiles' ouster broke.
Here is a preview.
(Begin VT)
ROSS DOUTHAT: There's a "Forbes" story that said that your net worth – maybe it's changed with the stock market recently – but your net worth went up by $3 billion since you returned to…
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): Well, so did everyone. OK, you ready? So, here's…
ROSS DOUTHAT: Everyone's – my net worth did not go up by $3 billion, for the record.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, you should have had stock.
ROSS DOUTHAT: I should have…
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: You should have had stock.
ROSS DOUTHAT: I should have had stock.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Excuse me. So, I devote – I devote…
ROSS DOUTHAT: How did it go up by $3 billion?
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, let me explain.

I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know. I have a son who's a very straight, good guy.
He watches over money. I don't even talk to him about it. He watches – he gives – they gave my money – I have a lot of cash. I have had a lot of cash long before I came in here.
ROSS DOUTHAT: Yes.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I don't take a salary, you know?
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you can watch that interview with President Trump on 60 Minutes tonight at 7:00 p.m.
We go now to Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren, the expected incoming Senate Banking Committee chair. And she joins us from Cambridge.
Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN (D-Massachusetts): Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you have written an outline here, an op-ed about what it's going to look like with Democrats in the majority.
You said: "Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who are unafraid to call out corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else."

That has echoes of President Trump's populist economic message, not what he said there, of course, but certainly what he has said to voters again and again. What specific policies do you think you can work with him on?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Look, President Trump himself said that he wants to reduce interest rates on credit cards to 10 percent. I got the bill. I'm ready to go.

President Trump says he wants to do more on housing. We're ready. We have the bills ready to go. And, besides that, we got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure that people have access to health care.

We have a lot of work lined out that we can do. In fact, one of the best parts of this election was how many Democrats stood up and didn't just say, I'm for the middle class. They said, here, I understand what is broken. Here are my specific plans to fix it, and I am committed to doing that.

So you end up with this situation where, in Michigan and Texas, you have got the candidates saying the same thing, break up big medicine. You end up with a situation where, in Kansas and in South Carolina, you have got the Democratic candidates saying, we love that ROAD to Housing bill, but we want to go bolder, bigger, more housing, a situation where, in North Carolina and Alaska, we have got candidates saying, hey, we need to break up the grocery monopolies and stop price gouging.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Iowa and Maine, where – where the Senate candidates there said, we're going to shore up Social Security and make billionaires pay their fair share.
And, you know, Margaret, those may sound like lots of different pieces.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: They're not. They're all about economic power.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: And people have told us that's what they want, and we have got the team to deliver now.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I mean, I don't have to tell you it's different to campaign than it is to actually legislate.

But President Trump has said he does want to work with Democrats on a few things here, immigration, tax cuts or – cuts or – quote – "maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient, a lot of economic development initiatives."
Does that track with your expectations of how this White House will be able to work with you, run by Stephen Miller and, of course, President Trump?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Look, let's be clear. The American people are the ones who've really set the agenda here. They're the ones who have told us what they wanted.
And they didn't just tell Democrats. They delivered a message to the Republicans pretty loud and clear.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: And I just follow through on what happened in the – just this last summer. We put together a bipartisan housing bill that is going to expand the supply of housing and help bring down the cost of housing…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: … and, for the first time ever in American history…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: … going to ban private equity.
Donald Trump didn't even sign the damn thing, and yet it is now law. We have got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be part of it or not.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you got a veto-proof majority on that particular bill. That's going to be perhaps more challenging.
You have said you want to bring big tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations who may have broken the law to face consequences. To be clear…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: … is your focus going to be legislation or is it going to be investigation?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Well, we have to do both.
But I do want to be clear. If you have been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who do you have in mind there when you say that?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Anyone who's been cheating. That's what investigations are all about.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK. So you don't have a list of people you plan to subpoena yet, you – even though you're going to be in this chair?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: I – it is important that we go through the steps for investigation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Because, look, the American people are just damn sick of this.
(CROSSTALK)

SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: They are sick of a White House that wouldn't enforce the laws even when they got cheated. They are sick of a White House that dropped investigations, that said, oh, if you make a nice contribution to Donald Trump's ballroom…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: … then there won't be any enforcement of the law when you have cheated millions of American customers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I want…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: That has to end.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Under – and we saw that in the polling, a concern about corruption.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Mm-hmm.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator Chris Coons, who is slated to take over Senate Foreign Relations in the new Congress, has said he wants questions answered about, it appears to be Nvidia, the chipmaker, and its CEO, Jensen Huang.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: "The New York Times" says he may have had a close relationship with a spy from China. Is there anything you can tell us about that? Is AI going to be a focus for you, and specifically this tech – this chipmaker?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Well, on the chipmaker specifically, this is an issue where we have actually substantial bipartisan support in the Banking Committee.
We have got – we have got Republicans and Democrats. I'm on bipartisan bills in order to put more restraints on the ability to export our chips to China.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: In fact, we have worked on a bipartisan basis to try to stop Donald Trump from encouraging Nvidia, permitting Nvidia to send these chips to China. And now we're seeing some of the consequences of that.
So we have got a lot of places where work needs to be done and a lot of different avenues to do it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well…
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: But the central part is going to be lowering costs for families and rooting out the corruption. It's not a long agenda.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, one of the things Democrats promised was to end the war with Iran. There are a few more weeks left in this Republican majority.
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You sit on the Armed Services Committee. There are senators like Senators Bennet and Senator Mark Kelly who have said something to the effect of Democrats should cut off funding for White House operations in order to pressure President Trump to end the war.

There are people in the House making noise like that. I mean, what does this look like? Are we looking at cutting off all government funding? Are we looking at a government shutdown in the next few weeks?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: Look, the pressure is building to end this war.

People have told us they want us to stop the war, a war that is illegal, that is halfway around the world, that to this day the Trump administration can't explain what their goals are and what their exit ramp looks like. They want us to stop it. They want us not to spend money over there.

They want to be able to buy gasoline and heating oil fuel, because they want this economy to work again. The way I think of this is, the wind is at our backs to end this war. We have got a lot of different tools on the table to get this done.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Leverage, you mean?
SENATOR ELIZABETH WARREN: But this is a democracy. And – yes.
And the American people have spoken. And it is time to listen to the American people. Democrats are ready to fight for that, and we invite the Republicans to join us.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We will watch for what that looks like.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, thank you for joining us today.
Face the Nation will be back in one minute. Stay with us.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Republican Congressman French Hill. He is currently the chairman of the Financial Services Committee, and he joins us from Little Rock, Arkansas.
Good morning to you, Congressman.
You survived a tough race down in Arkansas, usually ruby red. You finished just over 4,000 votes ahead of your Democratic rival. What went wrong for so many other of your Republican colleagues here?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL (R-Arkansas): Well, Margaret, it's good to be with you. It was a very complicated, tough election cycle this year.

Look, we told the American people in 2024 that we'd secure the border, we'd make our communities safer, we would lead in the world, but we also told the American people that we would continue to fight to lower costs.

And I think what we saw, no matter how many efforts that we made in the Republican House, that Americans are still concerned about the impact of 20 percent inflation that they experienced during the Biden administration, and that, while it's down from 9 percent to 3 percent, it has not gone lower.
And that I think was a principal issue, the costs that the American people are having and experiencing and all of our families.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: So, we have more work to do there.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, costs eating into wage gains, particularly over the past six months.

But let's talk about what's possible now. President Trump has changed his chief of staff, as you know, Stephen Miller now in that role. Your Republican colleague Don Bacon of Nebraska said Miller is not a good choice because he's antagonistic, he hurt Republicans during the election, saying he – quote – "took the immigration issue for President Trump from a 2-1 favorable to a 2-1 unfavorable."
Do you agree with him? I mean, what does putting Miller in the chief's role signal?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Well, first, I think Susie Wiles is leaving. President Trump has the right to promote Stephen Miller to be the chief.
That responsibility means that, during this 120th Congress, he will be the point person for the president in discussing policy matters with Congress.

I will tell you, though, on the immigration issue, I think we should focus on immigration reform, which I voted for twice back in 2018, to resolve the issues about how to seek asylum in this country, how we handle temporary protective services, and how we deal with children in this country that are here with legal green card holders, like our engineering community that's across the country, as well as those who've come in the country illegally, but their kids are legal.
We do need to resolve it. I think it's a place where President Trump can lead. And this is an area that Stephen Miller is keen on, which is secure the border, yes…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: … but can we now reform the immigration system and make it better for our country?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: And that will, I believe, answer the questions about the deportation issue.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I understand the aspiration, but, credibly, you believe Stephen Miller can persuade Democrats and be persuaded himself to go for the kind of asylum you just spoke about?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Well, look, this is what President Trump has said for years, that, if the border was secure, he wanted to try to reform our broken immigration system.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: And that was the – an issue that came up in his first term. This is an opportunity that perhaps we could, on a bipartisan basis, find that solution in the next Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

I – there's a lot of business for you all to get done. Your Republican colleague Thomas Massie is spearheading an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, the secretary. There is action expected this week. Some of your colleagues, like James Comer, has said: "With a high level of confidence there's a lot of questions about Hegseth, and Republican voters are upset."
Should Hegseth be impeached?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Well, the question is, for the president, should he continue to serve as the secretary of war?
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're going to be asked to answer this, though, by Representative Massie.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Yes, that's right.

Well I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment, versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president, if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War. That's the issue.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Are you satisfied with how the war has been handled?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: No. But, I mean, I think the commander in chief has to take the responsibility for the strategy of conducting the war and how it's been conducted.
But I will tell you one thing. There's nobody in America that wants Iran to have a nuclear weapon.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Of course not, right.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: This has been a goal of the United States for five decades.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Well, look at the 1990s, Margaret.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well…
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: President Clinton had the opportunity to prevent North Korea from having a nuclear weapon.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: And it didn't happen.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. And…
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: And that's a big issue for North Asia and for the U.S.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And CENTCOM just put out a $20 million reward offer for information about Iran's nuclear program. So it's clear the U.S. government doesn't have clarity, nor has it completely obliterated the program.
But just to go back to Hegseth, do I hear you right? You don't necessarily approve of how the war is going, but you're undecided about whether he has committed an impeachable offense?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Are you open to considering impeachment?

REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: Right, right. Here – look – look, this is – no, this is the issue. If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean, per se, that he's committed an impeachable offense.

He's an executive officer of the executive branch, and if he's not conducting his mission in the right way, then the president ought to make a change there. The question is, are we leading at the Pentagon in the right way or not the right way?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: That's very separate from whether or not somebody's committed an impeachable offense.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you don't want to commit on how you will vote today.
Have you reached a conclusion on whether you will vote for Steve Scalise or Jim Jordan for Republican leader?
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: These are two excellent leaders. They both could lead the conference successfully. We have, as you know, new members.

We have about 60, 65 members of our 170 majority that have only been in Congress two years or less. And I think we need to have our family meeting and discuss it. But both Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan are fully capable of leading in the minority, and I look forward to our discussion in conference this week.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right. Well, we will see who ends up, and we look forward to seeing how you end up voting on Secretary Hegseth as well.
French Hill joining us this morning from Arkansas.
REPRESENTATIVE FRENCH HILL: You bet.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Stay with us. A lot more Face the Nation when we're back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: In last week's midterms, nine out of 10 voters cited corruption as a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

Late last week, a former Trump White House official named Calley Means made allegations of corporate influence against a handful of top Trump officials, including now former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. His remarks were made in a podcast that dropped Friday and set off a firestorm in Washington.
Means is one of the leaders of the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement and helped form the alliance between RFK Jr. and Donald Trump in 2024. We spoke to him Saturday.
(Begin VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: President Trump has announced that Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has left the White House. The departure coincides with this resounding Republican loss in the midterms. But, also, you went public with some very specific allegations of corruption and a call to clean house.
Was it your intention to get her removed?
CALLEY MEANS (Former White House Senior Adviser): Yes.

I think President Trump has been subverted by people that are beholden to special interests and not what President Trump ran on and what voters voted for. I led the MAHA initiative at the White House. And Stephen Miller said it recently in a speech. The heart of MAHA is that we are the only primate, humans, that deal with pediatric cancer and rampant cancer rates.

And it's obviously because of our environment. It's because of pesticides. It's because of that 70 percent of a child's diet is ultra-processed food. It's because we're not out in the sun. It's basic, basic stuff.
And that, I think, was really the heart of the MAHA movement and I think a heart of what President Trump ran on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mm-hmm.
CALLEY MEANS: And there's very simple things. And Americans voted to change those things.

And I think, underneath Trump's nose, in many cases, you had a group of former lobbyists catering to the vaping industry, catering to the ultra- processed food industry, catering to the pharmaceutical industry, catering to the pesticide industry, and doing their bidding with an excuse that we need their money for the midterms and really need to actually go against what voters said, but we need their money.
Explicitly, that's what they said. And I think that…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mm-hmm. Who's they?

CALLEY MEANS: Susie and her cohort, Susie and Richard Walters, who is actually not someone most people know, but was one of the most powerful people in the country, was the de facto chief of staff when Susie was getting cancer treatment, Walker Barrett and James Blair, a very close-knit crew, who explicitly catered to special interests, against the will of the voters.

I think a lot of this happened without Trump's full knowledge. I don't think President Trump fully knew that some of these advisers were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against at the time they're giving explicit policy advice.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Directly taking money?
CALLEY MEANS: Directly, of course, yes.
Tony Fabrizio…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is a pollster.

CALLEY MEANS: … is one of the most powerful people in the country, and every single Cabinet secretary was conniving on how to convince Tony Fabrizio of their policy positions, because any policy went through Tony Fabrizio for a political check.
He was in the White House all the time, every single week. And…
MARGARET BRENNAN: He runs an outside polling firm that the White House relies on.
CALLEY MEANS: Yes, but that's a name. I mean, he was a – he was one of the most impactful players in White House policymaking, one of the most powerful people in the country.

He had a huge say in any policy that got done. And as he is opining on the political relevance of doing healthy food and healthy school lunches, or taking on the pesticide industry or taking on big pharma, which President Trump ran on, he was getting paid by Pfizer, by Pepsi, to this day. It's on his Web site right now.
You can see it on the Joe Rogan podcast I just did. We pulled up his Web site. It's advertised right now. He solicits clients right now and lists those people as his clients.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you think all of his polling is compromised?
CALLEY MEANS: I'm just stating facts. I'm just stating…
MARGARET BRENNAN: That that's your theory that you're putting forward.
CALLEY MEANS: Yes, I'm just stating a fact that we were trying to get a 90 percent support policy done of defining ultra-processed food.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
CALLEY MEANS: And he said, the juice isn't worth the squeeze on this, and advised against it, while being paid by Pepsi.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We have reached out to Tony Fabrizio for comment, and not heard back.

Richard Walters told CBS News he submitted his resignation Friday. Susie Wiles told us that – quote – "The president did more for MAHA than any president before or likely any president in the future."
We will be right back. More of our interview in the next half-hour.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will be right back with a lot more Face the Nation, in addition to more with Calley Means, and an interview with Democratic Congresswoman-Elect Nancy Lacore. She will be the highest-ranking female military officer to ever serve in Congress, joining what will be a record number of women veterans and women in the new Congress.
Stay with us.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to "FACE THE NATION."
Reaction to the announcement to Stephen Miller's promotion has been mixed, even among a handful of Republicans. We continue our interview with former White House Adviser Calley Means.
(BEGIN VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, RFK Jr., the HHS secretary, who you're very, very close to, said "Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It's time to unleash the Kraken."
What do you take that to mean?

CALLEY MEANS (Former White House Senior Adviser): What I take it to mean is actually an opening for Republicans and Democrats. Unleash the Kraken means doing things that matter to the American people. And when it comes to healthcare, these are completely nonpartisan things.

I mean, I spent every single day with Bobby Kennedy. As you said, probably more time with him than almost anyone. And what he says, what he pushes his team on is the exact same things that Democrats are running on. It is taking on corporate capture. It's taking on corruption. It's taking on big pharma incentives. It's making our food healthier. That is what he is pushing his team to do.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, on that point, I hear that you believe Stephen Miller is an ally to the cause. But in terms of an – being an operator in Washington, I mean he's radioactive to Democrats. They're already calling for him to be fired. He was the architect of the mass deportation policy that proved very unpopular in these midterms.
CALLEY MEANS: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Why do you think he can actually help you get things done on this cause.
CALLEY MEANS: Immigration, which is not my issue –
MARGARET BRENNAN: No.

CALLEY MEANS: I will say that a lot of polls said that that was one of – like actually solving the border crisis, Stephen Miller did do that. That was a core campaign promise. That was an existential issue. He is very competent and he has dramatically reduced those numbers. So, I can speak with most authority from the mob perspective.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

CALLEY MEANS: Let's talk about healthcare, Stephen Miller wants to get transformative things done with Bobby Kennedy and President Trump that are not partisan but structural. He wants to get the same things done that Elizabeth Warren and El-Sayed and other people are running on. And I think there is a major opportunity to come together and get some big things done, which, quite frankly, we have to do.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You told Joe Rogan that if you're a special interest group you pay Susie Wiles' daughter to get something done. What specific policy are you talking about here? What do you mean by that?
CALLEY MEANS: Margaret, everyone knows, including you, that this is how it works. They know that Continental Strategies, their revenue didn't go from zero dollars to $30 million a year by accident.
MARGARET BRENNAN: This is a political lobbying fund.

CALLEY MEANS: They – Ballard Partners, where Susie worked, became the highest revenue generating lobbying firm in the history of human civilization. That did not happen by accident. These companies that give those firms money are not acting irrationally. Like, more people – and I encourage more people to just say the truth. President Trump said the truth during the campaign. And this culture that Susie engendered was treating the American people like they're stupid and often, frankly, I think treating President Trump like he's stupid.
Obviously, Continental Strategies' revenues exploding was tied to Katie Wiles working there.
And what's an example? The fact that Katie was seen in an anti-American, pro-Russian government, Republika Srpska, recently and then magically leaders from that country have a meeting with Susie.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You do know, though, that there's been reporting that some of the president's own family members have their own financial interests and businesses here. You don't think that is compromising as well?

CALLEY MEANS: I think every question should be asked. Sure. I can't speak to that. What I can speak to is that I have never seen President Trump has a policy inclination against going aggressive on MAHA policies. And I can also substantiate that a lot of the things that have been slowed down were done under his nose.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, after Susie Wiles left, Secretary Kennedy publicly said she brokered his partnership with Trump. And then thanked her for helping to bring in disruptive leaders into HHS. He didn't say any of the things that you are saying here right now.

CALLEY MEANS: I feel very comfortable with what I said. I feel very comfortable with the hundreds of calls I've gotten from lawmakers and senior administration officials thanking me for what I've done.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did Secretary Kennedy know you were going to go public with these allegations?
CALLEY MEANS: No.
MARGARET BRENNAN: If you look at the recent MAHA conference that was just held here in Washington –
CALLEY MEANS: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: There were major corporations associated with it.
CALLEY MEANS: Right.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Walmart. UnitedHealthcare. And then there were also companies aligned with MAHA who have money to potentially make in peptide policy changes that Secretary Kennedy has, you know, championed. There are other wellness initiatives and people who financially could benefit from some of these policies. Doesn't that also risk compromising integrity?
CALLEY MEANS: I don't think – I don't think –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Those are also companies set to make money.
CALLEY MEANS: Yes. Yes. I can't speak for what an outside group does. I don't think any American thinks of Bobby Kennedy as compromised by special interests.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Were you comfortable with that?
CALLEY MEANS: No, I don't – I didn't want it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All those corporations being aligned?
CALLEY MEANS: I didn't want the framing of it. No. I – it's not – it was not my event. I didn't – I didn't love that. You're talking about one small conference and one small group.
MARGARET BRENNAN: It was pretty big.
CALLEY MEANS: I don't want the optic.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean the secretary spoke at it. Dr. Oz spoke at it.
CALLEY MEANS: I don't want the – I don't like the optic.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Russell Brand, the actor, whose –
CALLEY MEANS: I don't think any American thinks Bobby Kennedy is compromised. And I think every single corporate interest should be scrutinized.

But let's be honest, right, supplement companies aren't making Ballard Partners the highest revenue generating firm in the world, right? Peptide companies and compounders are not getting meetings with Ballard.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You have been in the crosshairs of some congressional Democrats who are now going to be in power in this new Congress. They've alleged you have your own conflicts of interest because you've owned between 25 to 50 million in stock in a company called True Med (ph) through November 2025. At that time I understand you had a different status. You were a special government employee. Then you became an employee, a permanent one, at the White House and some of the arrangements changed. But for those who look at that period of time, how can you address what they say are ethical issues that you had?

CALLEY MEANS: Yes. Everybody's conflicts should be highly scrutinized. I started a company to drive medical spending to exercise and healthy food after writing a book about exercise and healthy food. Through that advocacy I met Bobby Kennedy, met the Trump administration and was put into government. I became and SGE. And as you said, fully divested that company when I decided to go in full time. We raised around (ph) before the Trump administration started.
So, I started a company to promote healthy food and exercise and fully divested that company against my economic interests to come into government.
(END VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: A spokesperson for Continental Strategies, speaking for Katie Wiles, told us that, quote, "Mr. Means' claims regarding Continental Strategy are inaccurate and baseless," and said the firm has, quote, "never met with Mr. Means, lobbied for glyphosate, Monsanto, Baer (ph), vapes (ph), kratom (ph) or similar policies." Also that his allegations regarding Katie Wiles' participation in the Srpska elections are false, as has been previously reported, they say, by other media outlets.
We've also reached out to Ballard Partner, plus HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy and his aides for comment, but we have not heard back.
We'll be right back with the final part of our interview.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're back with the last part of our interview with Calley Means, which was taped Saturday morning.
(BEGIN VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: In a recent interview you said the administration was blocking health policies that you were trying to get passed. And you said specifically, they were doing it to take money from the sugar industry. You also talked about big tobacco. Explain that. What did you see?

CALLEY MEANS: So, last night, like yesterday, as Susie Wiles left, her deputies were still relentlessly pushing HHS to find a pathway for fruit- flavored vapes. The issues that came from Susie's world were not healthy food, were not, you know, cleaning up pesticides, were not, you know, these core issues that Bobby Kennedy ran on. I had to steamroll any of those policies through them with President Trump's support, you know, in using outside, you know, advocates, like Joe Rogan.
The issues that were being pushed hard in the previous regime were things like vapes, which are a huge donor to Ballard Partners. Are things like gas station heroin.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Kratom.

CALLEY MEANS: Marty Makary bravely put a high tolerance, you know, a low tolerance limit on those – on those products, which are causing devastation. You basically have opioids being sold at gas stations. He was pushed out and that tolerance limit was increased 20x so that there's still an ability for people to, you know, buy multiple products and get high, which was the direct intention of that policy. These are the types of policies that are being pushed – were being pushed. And again, we should be looking forward. It's a new day. But that's just demonstrably true.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The former FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary, resigned in May. And sources close to him said it was due to pressure from tobacco companies to make more available what you just said, fruit-flavored vapes. These e-cigarettes.

But there have been allegations that the president himself, Donald Trump, pressed for the FDA to allow more favorable policies for big tobacco because of donations to the political action committees for the midterms, that he himself knew.

CALLEY MEANS: I – maybe that's leaked by Susie. I don't know. I – what I saw a lot is that they would set up a quick meeting with President Trump. They would flag something, oh this is an important issue. He would say something and then they would jam it down, jam it down saying it's a president's priority for their priorities. I don't think President Trump ran, you know, as a primary purpose to help these industries.
MARGARET BRENNAN: No, he didn't run on it but –
CALLEY MEANS: I don't – and I don't think that's what he wants. Honest.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You don't think –
CALLEY MEANS: No, I don't. From –
MARGARET BRENNAN: He knew?

CALLEY MEANS: I don't think that's why he is serving as president. I think he talks to Bobby Kennedy about doing very transformational things. And what I know, and what I saw, is that there are systematic efforts, working with Ballard, working with these other people to help these industries. This was the single – this was the single most emphasized area for James Blair, who really led policy. You know, James Blair wasn't –
MARGARET BRENNAN: He's a political strategist.

CALLEY MEANS: James Blair wasn't pushing, you know, calling me in and saying, how can we, you know, promote more healthy food. How can we get more healthy food to kids? How can we, you know, talk about this MAHA principles? That never happened. I had to – I had to bulldoze to him. He was relentless on helping the fruit-flavored vape industry. So, that's what I saw.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, to that point. So, the tobacco company, Reynolds American, donated $5 million to a political action committee backed by Trump a week before the administration rolled out a new tobacco policy.

CALLEY MEANS: Yes, and that was a big reason why there was – that was a big argument from Susie's team on why we need to do this. That, you know, I didn't hear this specifically with vapes, but with the sugar industry I – you know, it was a direct conversation about how we need the sugar industry's money for the midterm. So, you know, when you have the midterm strategy and a belief that money for the midterms is more important than voter promises, you are basically able to excuse everything.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, "The New York Times" reported that tobacco lobbyists had actually been at the president's Florida golf course with him at lunch advocating to the president he picked up the phone and he called RFK Jr.
CALLEY MEANS: Yes, but –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did that happen?

CALLEY MEANS: I don't know. Brian Ballard was at that meeting, and I knew that Susie set up a lot of meetings with Brian Ballard to get a talking point, that the president support something. Again, I do not think fruit- flavored vapes or gas station heroin is any percentage of what President Trump is thinking about or wants to do.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because there is a pattern here. It was in the first Trump administration that the FDA tried to crack down on kratom, what you're calling gas station heroin. They also tried to crack down on fruit- flavored vapes. The FDA commissioner at that time, Dr. Scott Gottlieb, left.
CALLEY MEANS: And I said –
MARGARET BRENNAN: And yet in the second Trump administration, the very same issues are surfacing again. Are you sure the president isn't OK with it?

CALLEY MEANS: I am – I am sure that the president is – realizes that he has a generational coalition with Secretary Kennedy. He respects Secretary Kennedy. He wants to go hard on the issue of improving health for children. I think he had severe – poor advice from people I think who treated him like a baby in my respects and used him.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The president's staff treated him like a baby?

CALLEY MEANS: Of course. They would – they would block access to – and information to him all the time. I would be not surprised at all, you know, if they had very short conversations on these issues, you know, where the president is extremely busy and the president said, OK, whatever, and then they use –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Or he's not interested.
CALLEY MEANS: Yes, then they used that. Like it's all – it is all like the president wants this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Secretary Kennedy has endorsed Dr. Heidi Overton to be the next FDA commissioner. He said she's exceptionally dedicated, meticulous attention to detail, strategic leadership to every policy she touches. You accused her of writing a policy to relax standards on fruit- flavored vapes.

CALLEY MEANS: I'm not going to speak for Secretary Kennedy. Heidi Overton was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government on healthy food, on mental health treatments, like psychedelics. She was a stone wall and she really mindlessly, in my opinion, did whatever Susie told her to do.

Marty Makary was her mentor. And she, in a meeting, told Marty and I that she couldn't help Marty if he didn't approve a drug that he thought scientifically should not be approved, an mRNA flu vaccine. And it's just a factual statement that after Marty left, partly due to the vaping issue, she drove the creation of the relaxed vaping strategy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, in this new regime, with a the new chief of staff, do you think her nomination's going to be pulled? I mean she's already testified to Congress. She's still got to face a vote.
CALLEY MEANS: My opinion is Heidi Overton should not be – she does not have the character or integrity to be FDA secretary – or FDA commissioner.
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: A spokesman for Dr. Heidi Overton responded to Means' criticism of her qualifications and told CBS News that two former FDA commissioners think otherwise.

Dr. Marty Makary provided us the following statement, quote, "big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children. I wouldn't do it. The Kratom/7-OH lobby ran the same playbook to undermine my efforts to make this new 'gas station heroin' illegal. As FDA commissioner, I always rejected political corruption just as voters across the political spectrum did last week."
Now, we did also contact Susie Wiles, who told CBS that she had nothing to do with the tobacco industry meeting with the president at his golf club.

In response to Means' allegation, James Blair told CBS, quote, "I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all. I was tasked with driving FDA to make its process for approving or denying nicotine delivery device applications work the way current federal law dictates it works, which is that applicants get a yes or not approval in six months. Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely. Even though the president himself has made his position on spoking and smoking alternatives known very publicly and has provided clear direction. Calley just doesn't like it."
Now, President Trump has publicly stated that he saved flavored vaping during his first term to get people off smoking and he vowed in his second term to save vaping again, as you can see there.
More context and a full transcript will be available on our website. CBS News will continue to report on this evolving story.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We spoke Friday with Democratic Congressman-elect Nancy Lacore, a former Navy vice admiral and a mom of six who flipped a seat in South Carolina as part of last week's blue wave. She's a former registered Republican who says she left the party in 2016 because of President Trump. We began by asking her what areas she thinks she could work on with the president.
(BEGIN VT)

NANCY LACORE (Rep-elect, (D) South Carolina): I see a lot of opportunities because of what the new Congress is going to look like. You know, there's a significant majority this time. There are a lot of veterans who are now, you know, elected, you know, soon to be official congress men and women. And as veterans, we don't really care what your political affiliation is, we just focus on achieving the mission. And I think that's what you're going see out of this new Congress.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you said on the campaign trail that your mission would be bringing down the cost of housing, medical care, healthcare, getting rid of tax breaks for data centers. That's a long to-do list. You have a sense from Democratic leaders what the first initiative will be in the new Congress?

NANCY LACORE: The things that I'm going to focus on, on day one, first of all, will be to end this war, because that has driven up costs extraordinarily high across the district and the country. We also need to look at repealing some of these tariffs that have driven up a variety of other costs, including those of building new homes. And the one big, beautiful bill. There are some great pieces to the one big, beautiful bill, but there are some very – pieces that have done a lot of damage and made things a lot more unaffordable. I'd love to talk about the fact that we're not paying taxes on tips or Social Security, and I think that's great, but we need to make that permanent because right now those are going to expire with the end of this administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Nine out of ten voters said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote. They put it right up there with the cost of living.

Leader Jeffries, likely to be Speaker Jeffries, has said there should be accountability but, "the American people don't want us to get even, they want us to get things done because life is too expensive."
So, what does accountability look like? Do you need investigations or do you need legislation?

NANCY LACORE: It probably depends I think on what specifically we're talking about. We need to put some rules in place to make sure that our elected officials are not trading stocks. That is one area that we've seen I think extensive corruption there with insider information. But, you know, we also need to overturn, end Citizens United and make sure that we are getting that dark money out of politics so representatives can answer to their constituents and not, you know, insider interests.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, when we look at your bio, you will be the highest ranking female military officer ever to be elected to Congress. No female admiral or general has ever served before. You were chief of the Navy Reserve until you were relieved from your position by Secretary Hegseth in August 2025. He has said he's cutting the number of high-ranking officers by 20 percent, but he's also said he's ending diversity initiatives, or DEI. Do you have any idea why he targeted you?

NANCY LACORE: I don't. you know, I was never given a reason when I was removed from my position in August 2025. I don't think any of the other generals and admirals were ever given reasons either. And, frankly, at this point, it doesn't really matter. You know, it opened a door for me to do what I'm doing now and continuing my service in Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Secretary Hegseth released a video Thursday arguing that attempts to oust him from office are about his rebuilding of the force Here's a clip.
(BEGIN VC)

PETE HEGSETH (Defense Secretary): Diversity is not our strength. Our unity is. Men and women, they're not the same thing, but in the military they must be held to the same standard. Strong young men who believe in something greater than themselves are admirable.
(END VC)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Went on to call being transgender a mental illness. He dismissed a reference to white rage. He said that seemed to be maybe about renaming military bases and taking confederate general names off of them.
Of all of these initiatives, what do you think the impact has been on the U.S. military?

NANCY LACORE: You know, I've said since I launched this campaign, Pete Hegseth is the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen. He has caused significant damage to us as a country and put us at risk and really damaged the readiness of our entire military force. He is focused on the wrong things. He should be focused on strategy and readiness instead of these things that are down in the trenches.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, what do you think would be an impeachable offense? Because I know there is an effort underway in this Congress to do so. You've said you hope that gets taken care of before you come to Washington.

NANCY LACORE: Yes, I mean, I think there's probably plenty. And I do believe that this will be handled before I get there. You know, we can talk – we can tie this war as one thing that is extremely damaging to our country. Some of the things that we saw going on down – off Venezuela as well. But really it comes back to, you know, it's all a part of the problem with the corruption and the lack of strategy which is doing nothing but really driving up costs for people. And that's what people really care about. And so, that's what I want to focus on when I get to Congress.
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. Thank you all for watching. Until next week. For "FACE THE NATION," I'm Margaret Brennan.

title: ICE unlikely to scale back crackdown, sources say, citing Stephen Miller
summary: The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.
story: The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of immigration hawk Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Republicans suffered huge losses across the country on Election Day, including in some historically red states like Texas. Exit polls indicated that immigration was one of the top issues, alongside the economy, among Texas Latinos, who swung heavily toward Democrats. And 58% of voters nationwide said the Trump administration's deportation crackdown had "gone too far."

In January, Democratic lawmakers will take control of both chambers of Congress and assume sweeping powers to investigate the administration's immigration crackdown and its most controversial policies.

Still, officials at the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not received instructions to reduce immigration enforcement since the election, the sources said, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.

In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to try to carry out around 19,000 arrests per week, or about 2,700 per day, an increase from a prior 2,000 daily arrest target, agency sources told CBS News. That target was set before the midterms.

The U.S. officials cited Miller's appointment to the top post in the White House as a clear indication the Trump administration is likely to continue ICE's deportation blitz, as well as its quieter yet far-reaching campaign to sharply restrict legal immigration.
Asked if the midterms would usher in a pullback in immigration enforcement, one of the officials responded, "I would count on the opposite" with Miller as chief of staff.

The sources also said the administration believes the stunning electoral losses last week were largely driven by concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran — not its immigration crackdown.

"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorize our communities. There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News.

Bis cited the Trump administration's efforts to bolster security at the U.S.-Mexico border, where illegal crossings have plunged to historically low levels after soaring to record highs under former President Joe Biden's tenure.
In a statement Sunday, DHS said ICE would not be "backing away or slowing down."
"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets," DHS added.

Miller has been seen as a loyal foot soldier in Mr. Trump's inner circle for a decade, since his successful 2016 presidential campaign, when he promised to shut down Muslim immigration to the U.S. and dramatically expand deportations of those in the U.S. illegally.

During that time, Miller has solidified himself as the chief architect of Mr. Trump's hardline immigration policies. Miller was one of Mr. Trump's top aides during his first administration, when officials banned immigration and travel from Muslim-majority countries and separated thousands of migrant children from their parents as part of a "zero tolerance" crackdown that was abandoned after massive public uproar.
But Miller has greatly expanded his power — and his influence over federal immigration policymaking — since Mr. Trump's return to the White House.

In less than two years, with Miller as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, the second Trump administration has effectively closed the U.S. asylum system; shut down refugee admissions, with a notable exemption for White South Africans; tightened access to different legal immigration benefits like green cards; and undertaken highly visible ICE and Border Patrol arrest operations across the country.

Those immigration enforcement operations have often triggered widespread community backlash, including in January, when federal immigration officials killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during a crackdown in Minneapolis that the administration scaled back following bipartisan outcry.

Miller has publicly floated the idea of suspending habeas corpus — the conditional right for people to challenge unlawful detention — for ICE detainees. Habeas cases have skyrocketed over the past two years, as the Trump administration has greatly narrowed other avenues for those fighting deportation to be released from ICE detention.

In addition to his immigration portfolio, Miller has also played an influential role in the Trump administration's crackdown on universities and legal groups, and its campaign to investigate allegations of fraud in Democratic-led states like Minnesota.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said the Trump administration's deportation efforts are likely to face some obstacles next year. She expects congressional Democrats to use their new powers to try to rein in ICE, including by issuing a flurry of subpoenas, holding oversight hearings and passing measures to limit immigration enforcement funds.

Cardinal Brown also predicts that some communities and states with newly elected Democratic leaders, like Texas, may scrap or limit policies that allowed or required local law enforcement officials to work with ICE. Last week, Houston's mayor said he would direct local police to limit their cooperation with ICE, following the election results.

But Cardinal Brown stressed that Mr. Trump will likely veto any Democratic attempts to restrict ICE enforcement and noted the agency received $75 billion in funds through 2029 due to the "One Big Beautiful Bill" that the president signed into law last year.
"They're going to continue apace," Cardinal Brown said. "They have the money. They have the resources."

title: The SS United States and her final destination
summary: She was the fastest ocean liner in history. But the jet age took the SS United States out of service, and she wound up docked in Philadelphia for nearly 30 years. Now, she's scheduled to be scuttled off Florida, to become the world's largest artificial reef.
story: Even with her paint peeling and rivers of rust, the queen of the North Atlantic – five city blocks long, 12 stories high – still strikes quite a pose in the setting sun. The SS United States quickly became the fastest ocean liner in history. On her maiden voyage back in 1952, she reached speeds topping more than 40 miles an hour – a record for a transatlantic crossing that's never been broken.
But she was elegant, too – stately and refined. During her nearly two decades in service, she carried four U.S. presidents, countless celebrities, and tens of thousands of happy voyagers.

But what was once glamorous and spacious, the jet age did away with. Speed won out over starry nights at sea. By 1969, the SS United States was withdrawn from service, and that's what gets us back to her currently forlorn state. She wound up in Philadelphia, where for almost 30 years she sat with only spiders and sunbeams booking passage.
But she was still impossible to ignore.

"She still casts a spell; there's something about her," said Susan Gibbs, president of a non-profit called the SS United States Conservancy. "She has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together."

Gibbs knows every inch of this ship. Her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the SS United States, with the U.S. military helping to foot the bill – a floating investment that could be converted in less than 24 hours into a troop ship to transport an entire division. "It may not seem that way now, but back then she was the space shuttle of her age," Gibbs said.
Only her bones are left, however – her once-grand staircase is bare; the indoor salt-water swimming pool is now just a ghostly abyss; the dance floor is still here, but nothing else.
And yet, there was still enough that Gibbs was determined to save. There were all kinds of ideas – museums, restaurants, event spaces – but no takers.

Our one-time flagship seemed headed for the scrap heap. Until that is, one man had a wild idea: return the SS United States back to the Atlantic, not to sail, but to sink – sending her to the bottom of the sea where nature, instead of the wrecking ball, will take its course.
"This will be the largest purposely-sunk artificial reef in the world," said Alex Fogg.

As the natural resources chief for Okaloosa County, Florida, Fogg has sunk a lot of ships – in fact, dozens of them, smaller ones off the coast of Florida as part of the county's artificial reef program.

The vessels have created habitats that are a delight for fish, fisherman and frogmen alike. But sinking the SS United States is something entirely different. Just one look at her two massive engine rooms and you realize the enormity of the task ahead.

For Jennifer Adams, director of tourism for Okaloosa County, what better tourist attraction could she bring? When she was approached about buying the SS United States, she said her response was, "'How much?' And he told me and I said, 'Go get her.'"
That price tag? A mere $1 million for the legendary ship, plus another $13 million to ready her for sinking. But then, the idea of sinking her suddenly became a little too real.
"I cried this morning when I walked on board," Adams said. "I just, I got overwhelmed."

Her county now owned a historic ship, but one full of 1950s environmental contaminants; that's problem one. Problem two was the SS United States still had plenty of fans on land, people like Linda Sylva, who made her first voyage as a teenager. "She was made in America, made from American parts, all over America," Sylva said.

Joe Beaman was just an eight-year-old kid when he set sail. All these years later, he's never forgotten it. "Oh no, once that ship has your heart, you never lose it," he said. "I mean, it's a part of me."
Even those who never sailed on her, like Jeffrey Smith, felt some kind of pull: "I drove in from Detroit yesterday because I wanted to say goodbye."
He and the others were on a farewell cruise of sorts, organized by the Conservancy, to give fans one last look before her last port of call.
In 2025, crews cast off her lines and began towing the SS United States south, her funnels barely clearing Philadelphia's Walt Whitman bridge.
Once at sea, she had all the majesty she always did, cutting the waves like a scalpel. She arrived almost two days ahead of schedule. "She's still breaking records, even today," Fogg laughed.

At a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama, she's undergone extensive remediation, from stem to stern, getting rid of those environmental contaminants. Holes were cut throughout to allow air and water to flow quickly and evenly during her sinking.
If all goes well, she'll be scuttled this week about 20 nautical miles off the coast between Pensacola and Destin/Ft. Walton Beach, Florida.

Her two funnels – some of the largest ever built – will become the bookends of a museum planned by the SS United States Conservancy that will eventually house one-of-a-kind artifacts, including the bar from the tourist class smoking lounge.
There will be plenty of salty tears when she's gone. Sinking seems contrary to everything she was designed to do. That said, the SS United States will remain a part of maritime lore forever.
After so many years alone, soon she'll become a place of life once again.

"She stood there year after year after year," said Linda Sylva, "waiting for somebody to say, 'Come here, you're welcome here.' And who is that welcome for? It's the ocean. What a perfect place for her to rest."

title: Villa Vie Odyssey "forever cruise" residents want their ship back
summary: Some residents of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise are trying to reclaim the ship, which could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned.
story: As the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship makes its way from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned of at least two resident-led efforts to reclaim the vessel.

One effort recently failed after a lender denied funding to residents of the luxury "forever cruise." However, a second effort to buy the ship is still very much active, according to two sources familiar with the matter. It is led by another group hoping to buy the ship at auction, the sources said.
The second effort would not involve Villa Vie Residences' founder and executive chairman Mike Petterson, according to sources involved in the discussions.
Petterson said he believed he had an operational partner to rescue the ship, but that did not pan out, which led to the ship being taken by its lender.

Now, Petterson says he believes he could still get the ship back and is continuing to look for potential investors to take over the ship for good. Another option would be to raise the funds to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and sell the company. He no longer wants to be involved in company leadership.
"I'm not going to be the front face person of a company any time soon," Petterson told CBS News.

CBS News has also learned that a group of residents is considering legal action over fuel loans that were provided to the company in April — when residents said they raised more than $2 million dollars to keep the ship afloat.
The fuel loan program promised up to a 24% return if residents invested more money to help with the rising cost of fuel.
In a copy of an agreement obtained by CBS News, which appears to be from Villa Vie, the loan is described as "Unsecured" without "Collateral or Guarantees."

Craig and Cindy Voight were on board the ship from October 2024 when the Odyssey departed Belfast, Northern Ireland, for its voyage around the world. The couple said they spent more than $300,000 on their cabin and monthly dues, in addition to providing the company with $100,000 as participants in the fuel loan program. They said they plan to take legal action over that program.

"So we thought, alright, we're going to get 18% interest," Craig Voight said.  "First payment's supposed to start a month later. So between then and now they owe us over $113,000. They've never paid one penny."
Petterson acknowledged that some residents could potentially take legal action over the fuel loans in a statement that he shared with CBS News, saying "I take their concerns seriously."

In his statement, the executive also said financing for the loan program "was arranged during an urgent period for the vessel and was intended to support immediate operating needs, including fuel." The financing was structured through Villa Vie's parent company, Residential Cruise Holdings, "because existing financing restrictions prevented Villa Vie Residences from borrowing directly," he said.

"I recognize that residents want clear answers about how the loans were structured and handled," said Petterson. "Because legal action is being considered, I won't discuss individual claims or draw conclusions in the media. We will address the matter through the appropriate legal process and provide information through the proper channels."
This story published first on CBS News at 8:28 a.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

title: 1 dead, at least a dozen hurt after car strikes cyclists in North Carolina
summary: One person was killed and at least a dozen others injured when a driver suspected of being impaired struck a group of more than 40 cyclists in North Carolina, authorities said.
story: One person was killed and several others injured Saturday morning when a driver suspected of being impaired struck a group of more than 40 cyclists in North Carolina, authorities said.

According to North Carolina State Highway Patrol, a little after 9:30 a.m. Eastern time a black Infiniti passenger car was traveling west on a road in Wake County when it crossed the center line and crashed into a group of cyclists who were biking east.
The driver did not stop at the scene, but continued for about a half-mile before crashing into a ditch on the side of the road, state highway patrol said.

Holly Springs Fire Chief LeRoy Smith said seven people were transported to a hospital with major injuries and 15 others sustained minor injuries. State highway patrol pegged the injury toll at about a dozen, however.
The deceased victim was identified by state highway patrol as 63-year-old Patrick Allen Turner of Cary, North Carolina.

The suspected driver, 76-year-old Donald Robert Morris-Jones of Apex, North Carolina, was arrested on multiple charges, including felony death by vehicle, felony serious injury by vehicle, felony hit-and-run involving serious injury or death, reckless driving and driving while impaired, according to officials.
He is being held on $1 million bond.
People at the scene told Smith the cyclists were part of a group that regularly gathers for weekend bike rides.
Wake County is located about 14 miles southwest of Raleigh.

title: 2 licensed skydivers die after midair collision in California
summary: The two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet above the ground, Skydive Elsinore said.
story: Two female skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.

The accident occurred Friday and involved two licensed, experienced skydivers at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement. The Riverside County Sheriff's Department said deputies were dispatched late Friday morning after reports of an air emergency. The skydivers were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries.
They were pronounced dead at the hospital, the sheriff said.
The Riverside County coroner's office later identified the victims as 29-year-old Levi Pimentel of Aurora, Illinois, and 56-year-old Georgia Jean of Box Elder, South Dakota.

Skydive Elsinore said the free-fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at about 150 feet above the ground.

"The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground," Skydive Elsinore said in a statement.  The company said there was no evidence of equipment malfunction.
The skydivers were visiting from out of town to take part in an organized skydiving event, the company said.
Skydive Elsinore — which says they are the longest-running skydiving operation in North America —  is located approximately one hour away from both San Diego and Los Angeles metropolitan areas.

title: What Stephen Miller has pushed for while in Trump administration
summary: Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations.
story: Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations.
Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term.

The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies.

Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025.

During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time. Under former President Barack Obama, the ceiling was 110,000 for fiscal year 2017.
Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship.

In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes.
He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations.

Miller's arrest targets were part of a sweeping expansion of enforcement in communities, workplaces and immigration courts. Detentions of immigrants without criminal histories rose sharply, and increased ICE activity sparked protests across the country.

The longtime Trump adviser also championed the use of a wartime law — the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — to bypass due process and quickly deport alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held in a notorious maximum-security prison, known as CECOT. The deportations set off a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the government from immediately deporting the Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal.

As part of the administration's deportation efforts, Miller has supported an aggressive expansion of third-country deportations. The administration has deported immigrants to countries where they have no citizenship or family ties, including several African nations.
In May 2025, Miller said the administration was actively considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court.
At a March 2026 conference in Miami, Miller argued that military force, rather than traditional criminal law enforcement alone, was needed to defeat cartels.

Miller appeared alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office this summer as he signed executive orders to refuse citizenship to some children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier executive order aiming to end birthright citizenship.

title: Pope voted in U.S. election because he's "proud to be an American"
summary: Pope Leo, who is on a 12-day, three-country trip in Latin America, also said he credits God and doctors for his lung cancer surgery recovery.
story: Pope Leo XIV, who became the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election, said Friday he is "proud to be an American and to exercise my right" to vote.

His remarks, made to reporters en route to Latin America for a 12-day trip, come after the Vatican confirmed the U.S.-born pontiff had voted via mail-in ballot in his native Chicago. He declined to comment on the outcome of the midterm elections, which gave control of Congress to the Democrats in a repudiation of President Trump. Instead, he pointed to the statement released by the Vatican last week that cited his longstanding belief in civic participation.
The pope, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said in an Oct. 30 statement.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican said in a statement.

The pope has a long history of civic engagement in the U.S., the Vatican said, confirming that during his nearly two decades as a missionary and then bishop in Peru, Leo voted whenever he was eligible. He holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
The Associated Press reported Leo, as Robert Prevost, previously voted in five primary elections since 2000 — on the Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2019 and Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
Leo said Friday that he hadn't been able to vote in Peru's recent election since absentee ballots "aren't possible."
"But I would have done it. It's a good thing," he said, according to the AP.
U.S. federal law allows American citizens, even those who work for foreign governments, to retain their citizenship.

The 71-year-old pope is on a three-nation, 12-day tour just three weeks after he underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. He was cleared to travel on Oct. 26 — two weeks after his surgery.

"I am very happy to be here myself. I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place," Leo told reporters when he greeted them in the back of the plane. "I confess that from the first day, I had no doubt. I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape."
He acknowledged, though, that he hadn't had a chance to play tennis yet.
"Not yet, but I will," he said.

On Oct. 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of Leo's right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.

"Early detection is obviously the best way to go, and so regular checkups are a blessing," Leo said, crediting his recovery to "trusting God, good doctors, good surgeons, and overall I think a healthy lifestyle."
