title: 11th-hour power play targets incoming Dem governor after historic GOP defeat
summary: Republican Texas Rep. Brian Harrison urged Greg Abbott to convene a special session restricting emergency powers before Gina Hinojosa is sworn in.
story: Fox News host Will Cain breaks down the stunning Texas governor race upset where Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats incumbent Governor Greg Abbott on ‘The Will Cain Show.’
A GOP lawmaker in Texas is seeking to limit some of the incoming governor's powers after Democrats flipped the state blue in Tuesday's election.

Republican Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison on Wednesday publicly urged outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott to convene a special session to "rein in" the governor's executive emergency powers before Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office.

"Republicans lost last night, but Democrats were not sworn in," Harrison wrote in a lengthy statement posted on X. "We still have total power in Texas, and we must act like it by using the remaining ten weeks to restore separation of powers and limit the emergency powers that Governor-Elect Hinojosa is set to inherit, that would allow her to destroy liberty in Texas by executive fiat."
Harrison also emphasized in the post that he believes Texas governors should not have "unchecked" emergency powers, regardless of their party affiliation.
TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES
The Texas State Capitol in Austin. (AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

"Texas should have reined in executive emergency powers when I first demanded it in 2022," Harrison told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "If these are not revoked, Gina Hinojosa will assume not just the powers our state constitution bestows upon a Governor, but will, in effect, inherit nearly all the powers of a dictator. Most people are shocked to learn Texas governors can write, edit, or change any statute on a whim if they just declare an ‘emergency,’ and this is unconstitutional."

Under Section 433.002 of the Texas Government Code, the governor may issue emergency directives and "amend, modify, or rescind" those directives during a declared state of emergency, subject to the requirements outlined in the law.

"These powers have been abused in the past, and Governor-Elect Hinojosa has pledged to use them on day one," the Texas Republican added. "Republicans are still in control for ten weeks, we need to start acting like it."

Harrison also said in the X post that the Texas Legislature should "immediately pass" legislation such as HB911, which he filed in December 2022 to restrict the governor’s "never ending emergency powers."
His comments come after Hinojosa defeated Abbott in Texas' 2026 gubernatorial race on Tuesday, becoming the state's first Latina governor.

While on the campaign trail, Hinojosa pledged that she would declare "a high-cost emergency" in Texas and introduce executive orders to halt the state's gas and diesel taxes and to freeze residential electricity rates, the Texas Tribune reported Wednesday.

A split image shows Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa in the 2026 Texas gubernatorial race. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Abbott's office and Hinojosa's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

In a Thursday X post, Harrison claimed that his demand to curb the Texas governor's emergency powers "has REALLY triggered low-IQ leftists across America," adding that he did not "recall them cussing and calling me every name in the book when I filed the same legislation 4 years ago... right after ABBOTT was re-elected!!"

The governor of Texas possesses the ability to sign or veto bills passed by the state's Legislature, serve as commander in chief of the state's military forces and convene special legislative sessions "for specific purposes," according to Abbott's office.

Under the Texas Disaster Act of 1975, the governor can declare a state of disaster and exercise certain emergency powers, including suspending specific regulatory requirements, but disaster declarations must be renewed after 30 days and can be terminated by the Legislature at any time.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Hinojosa vowed in a Wednesday X post that her administration will "lead with a politics of courage, not convenience."
The Democratic Party notched another key victory in the Lone Star State on Tuesday after James Talarico toppled Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race.

Ahead of Hinojosa taking office next year, some Republican Texas state senators have pledged to "hold the line" against Democrat-led policy goals in the state, The Houston Chronicle reported Wednesday.
State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, speaks during an education town hall at a community center on Oct. 10, 2026, in Cypress, Texas. (Danielle Villasana/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted Abbott in a Truth Social post, claiming the governor lost his re-election bid because he is a "RINO," an acronym that stands for "Republican in name only."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost," Trump wrote in the social media post. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!"
After conceding the race, Abbott told supporters on Tuesday that he had informed Hinojosa that he "would assist her and her team in a period of transition," The Hill reported.

"For weeks, I had been publicly warning on this podcast that we were in very real danger of losing everything in Texas," Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz said Wednesday in an X post. "Far too few believed that was possible. I am very, very sorry that it came to pass. Texas has not had a Democrat governor since 1994."
"We haven’t had a Democrat senator since 1993," Cruz added. "Now we’ll have both."
Hinojosa is set to officially take office in January 2027.

title: Trump ‘holds all the cards’ in war against Iran’s regime, White House says
summary: Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei taunts America after midterms, but the White House says Trump holds all the cards on the Strait of Hormuz.
story: Iran remains a major focal point as President Donald Trump reveals he will 'finish the job' against Iran if the regime doesn't behave. Former NSC Chief of Staff Alex Gray also joins 'Fox & Friends First' discuss the conflict.

JERUSALEM — With Iran’s missing-in-action Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei taunting Americans about the "collapse" of the U.S. after the midterm elections, the White House and Middle East experts argue President Donald Trump is positioned to defeat the remnants of the rogue regime.

The remaining two years of Trump’s Iran policy have profound implications for his legacy and could lay the foundation for a new Middle East devoid of the region’s worst state sponsor of terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, should Trump pursue new military actions to dislodge Khamenei’s regime, according to experts.

Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since a joint U.S.-Israel airstrike killed his father, former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and members of his family, boasted on X following the Republican defeat in the midterms: "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since a joint U.S.-Israel airstrike killed his father. (Vahid Salemi/AP; Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP)
IRAN TAKES A VICTORY LAP OVER STUNNING US ELECTION RESULTS, CLAIMS 'COLLAPSE HAS ACCELERATED'
The radical Islamist clerical ruler’s braggadocio was met with tough statements from the White House and leading Middle East experts on Iran’s theocratic state.

A White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."
TRUMP REVIVES IRAN REGIME CHANGE SPECULATION WITH CRYPTIC CALL FOR PEOPLE TO 'RISE UP'
The spokesperson added, "Only President Trump knows what he will do and when."

The Islamic Republic ramped up its bellicose anti-American and anti-Western rhetoric and activities over the last week. Tehran presented a "Trump in a Cage" exhibit with a mock execution of Trump to coincide with the regime’s anniversary of its illegal seizure of the U.S. Embassy and kidnapping of its personnel on Nov. 4, 1979.
Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei attends a meeting in Tehran, Iran, in this photo from March 2016. (Rouhollah Vahdati/ISNA/WANA/Reuters)
TRUMP CALLS IRAN CONFLICT A 'SOFT WAR,' INSISTS US HOLDS THE CARDS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS

The ayatollahs did not restrict their jingoism to the U.S. An AI-generated video published by state-controlled Iranian media outlets shows the spokesperson of the headquarters of the Islamic Republic of Iran Armed Forces threatening Western Europe.

"We are not like you," the spokesperson said. "Iran does not harm innocents. You are not our enemy. But anyone, anywhere in Europe, who assists America in harming our women and children is our enemy, and we will punish them."
The video features military targets in France, Germany and Britain.

Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital that Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, went so far as to claim that Iran had inflicted a political defeat on Trump in Washington, in addition to its supposed victories on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf similarly portrayed the election results as an American rejection of the war," Mohebbi said.
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran alongside several Cabinet members on Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)
TRUMP CAN’T LET IRAN TURN A MILITARY DEFEAT TURN INTO A DIPLOMATIC VICTORY
He argued it was part of a broader psychological and political campaign.

"Tehran, along with commentators sympathetic to the regime in the United States, is trying to promote the wildly exaggerated narrative that confronting the Islamic Republic carries an unbearable electoral cost for American politicians," Mohebbi said. "Evidence does not support the claim that the Iran war alone caused the Republican defeat. According to national exit polling, only 4% of voters identified foreign policy as the country’s single most important issue."
The phrase "finish the job" has become synonymous with toppling the 47-year ironclad totalitarian rule of the Islamic Republic.
IRAN’S REGIME WON’T NEGOTIATE IN GOOD FAITH. TRUMP MUST BREAK ITS GRIP
"I believe President Trump should finish the job, because the fundamental threats posed by the Islamic Republic remain unresolved," Mohebbi said, adding the nuclear file is far from closed.

"Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile remains unaccounted for under international verification, and the regime has retained the ability to rebuild elements of its ballistic missile program," he said. "More importantly, its underlying strategic behavior and hostility toward the United States and its regional allies have not fundamentally changed."

Former Pentagon official Simone Ledeen told the London-based Iran International news organization the Islamic Republic "needs to end" and the regime will never change its behavior. She called for support for Iran’s people on the ground and opposes putting American troops on the ground.
TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME

Veteran Iran observers and experts have noted Trump was the first U.S. leader not to kick the Iran nuclear weapons problem down the road. His decision to confront Iran’s illegal atomic weapons system was one of the most decisive foreign policy achievements of his administration, according to popular American commentators like Ben Shapiro.
Shapiro termed Trump’s Operation Epic Fury campaign against Iran "the single bravest foreign policy move of my lifetime."

"What you’re watching him [Trump] do in Iran is not only unprecedented in terms of its political courage. I think that it is and has the potential to be a true game changer for America’s role in the world, not only for the next 10 or 20 years, but for the coming century," Shapiro told Lara Trump on Fox News' "My View" in March.
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

Mohebbi said there is also a critical factor that Washington must understand: the Islamic Republic is attempting to wait out the Trump administration. Even if Trump were to negotiate the strongest possible agreement today, he believes Tehran would view it as a temporary arrangement rather than a permanent change in its strategic direction.

"The regime calculates that a future Democratic administration would not resort to military action against it," he said. "Once Tehran believes the threat of military force is off the table, it will become even more defiant in its behavior and more brazen at the negotiating table."
Another school of thought is to subcontract military actions to Israel against Iran’s regime.
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran on Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)
IRAN REGIME CHANGE TALK RESURFACES AS TRUMP SAYS TEHRAN 'WANTS TO MEET' AMID US STRIKES
Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital that Tehran's strategy has always been to wait out U.S. pressure.

"They were hoping to ride out the Trump administration's pressures for two more years. Now they believe they have it," Soghom said. "I think he should give full support to Israel to do the job and not interfere. The U.S. should continue to maintain its blockade of Iran and facilitate shipping from the Persian Gulf, but except hitting well-protected and highly dangerous targets, such as nuclear sites if needed, the U.S. should stay out of continuous attacks because its internal political situation is messed up."
Soghom, who tracks Iranian regime media, added the Iranian state radio is celebrating the Democratic victory.

"Incidentally, 47 years ago today, the new Islamic regime in Tehran gave the green light to its supporters to attack and seize the U.S. embassy," he said. "This election result will embolden them, and they'll not be inclined to compromise with the Trump admin — or even a future Democrat. Like in most other things, Trump did not finish the job when he could."

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that Iran sees the midterm election results as exacting a political cost from the Trump administration for launching Operation Epic Fury.

"It hopes these electoral losses will deter this and future administrations from launching military operations against Tehran over its aggression and terrorism," Brodsky said, adding that at the same time, Iranian decision-makers are likely eyeing Trump warily.
"President Trump has proven unpredictable and, with over two years left in office, that is a lot of time for the U.S. to continue to damage the Iranian regime," Brodsky said.

He noted that while Congress can complicate and raise objections, historically, without a veto-proof majority, it retains limited options for checking executive branch operations in this space.
"The 2006 midterm elections are instructive here, where, despite the prevailing anti-war sentiment at the time, President Bush still authorized a surge in the Iraq War," Brodsky said.

title: Democrats’ midterm sweep opens path to bypassing Electoral College by 2028
summary: Democrat trifectas in key swing states could push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past 270 electoral votes needed to activate it and thus change the way Americans select the presidency.
story: Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discusses criticism of the Electoral College by former 2026 Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris on ‘America Reports.’
Democrats’ midterm gains have opened a new front in the fight over how America chooses its president — one that could reshape the 2028 race for the White House.

Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, already enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C., has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. If the four states join, their combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it. Arizona could push the total to 283 if Democrats ultimately gain control of both chambers there.

National Popular Vote (NPV), the nonprofit organization that authored the compact and is campaigning to enact it state by state, says it has identified multiple legislative sponsors in each of the five states whose combined electoral votes could push the compact over the 270-vote threshold. It expects bills to be pre-filed before, or introduced early, in the 2027 legislative sessions.
"I am confident we have multiple paths to secure the 48 electoral votes required to deliver what 63% of Americans want," Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant for NPV, told Fox News Digital.
VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS
A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the current electoral system, every state except Maine and Nebraska awards its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the statewide vote. If the compact takes effect, participating states would instead award their electors to the candidate who wins the most votes nationwide, leaving the Electoral College formally in place but making the national tally decisive.

Supporters argue the compact would give every vote equal weight by counting ballots toward a single national total. The Electoral College, by contrast, was structured to give both populous and smaller states a meaningful role in choosing the president.

"They can’t use a compact to, in essence, change the Electoral College," Hans von Spakovsky, an election law expert with the conservative group Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital when asked about the potential activation of the compact before the 2028 election.

"This is unprecedented," von Spakovsky, a former commissioner on the Federal Election Commission (FEC), continued. "In the past, the only kind of compacts that have been agreed on between states have been things like water sharing — when rivers run between states, they enter into compacts to agree on that. But a compact that changes a fundamental structural given in the Constitution, I think the Supreme Court would say you can’t do that."
HILLARY CLINTON STILL FUMING OVER ELECTORAL COLLEGE, CALLS IT AN 'ABOMINATION' IN NEW NETFLIX SERIES
A fourth grader works on an election-themed art project at Heather Hills Elementary School in Bowie, Md., on Oct. 22, 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Rosenstiel rejected the argument that the compact would improperly alter the Constitution, saying NPV believes Article II, Section 1 gives states the authority to determine how their presidential electors are appointed.

"Any clean read of Article II, Section 1 makes it clear that states have the exclusive power to award electors," Rosenstiel said. "The only credible legal question is whether this compact requires congressional consent."

Von Spakovsky argued that because the NPV compact is an agreement between states, Congress would have to approve it under the Constitution's compact clause in Article I. He noted Congress could approve the compact with simple majorities in the House and Senate and that the Constitution does not explicitly require the president’s signature — meaning a presidential veto might not stop it.
However, von Spakovsky added that states choosing not to participate in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would have a strong basis for litigation.

"Given that the NPV is entirely a creation of Democrats and only supported by Democrats, the new Congress will no doubt easily pass this compact," he told Fox News Digital. "However, I believe the non-participating states would have a good basis for litigation, which would end up in the Supreme Court, arguing that the compact is unconstitutional because it changes a fundamental structural part of the Constitution without going through the constitutional amendment process. The argument would be that states cannot make agreements among themselves that damage the federal system provided by the Constitution."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Challenges to the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact could end up at the Supreme Court. (Getty Images)

National Popular Vote’s campaign has identified sponsors in all five potential additions following the midterms that could help push the compact over its 270-vote threshold and plans to begin pushing bills before or early in the 2027 legislative sessions, according to Rosenstiel.

Rosenstiel said the compact would apply to the 2028 election only if states representing at least 270 electoral votes join before July 20 of that year. That gives state lawmakers, Congress — if approval is required — and the courts less than two years to resolve the political and constitutional questions.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Until then, the Electoral College remains unchanged.
"I’m increasingly confident we can achieve that goal and we will have a national popular vote for president in 2028. I would certainly prepare for it," he said.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: MAGA voters reveal who they want to see lead GOP in 2028
summary: MAGA voters at a Trump rally name JD Vance and Marco Rubio as early 2028 presidential election favorites after Democrats swept the midterms.
story: Vance or Rubio? MAGA voters speaking with Fox News Digital ahead of a recent Trump rally reveal their early picks for 2028 Republican presidential nomination

With Democrats taking control of Congress in the midterm elections, MAGA voters are already sizing up potential successors to President Donald Trump in 2028 — with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeatedly emerging as favorites among those interviewed by Fox News Digital.
"I like [Rubio]," one American told Fox News Digital. "I like that he's no-nonsense, similar to Trump."
"Well, I like JD Vance obviously," another said. "I like Marco Rubio. There's some other ones, too, that are maybe not so much mainstream that are coming up that I like too."
TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028

Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are gaining traction among American voters as potential favorable 2028 presidential candidates for Republicans. (Annabelle Gordon/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Kylie Cooper/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"JD is great too, but Rubio has a little more experience," one said. "He's articulate, he’s well-spoken. He's got good ideas. I just really like him."

Fox News Digital spoke with Americans attending a Trump rally in Port Huron, Michigan, as one of Trump’s final stops before Tuesday’s midterms that ended in a stunning blue wave. Fueled by anger over high costs and the war with Iran, Americans voted to oust Trump and his agenda, boosting Democrats to large majorities in the House and Senate.
With Democrats looking to rebuke Trump and his allies, Republicans that Fox News Digital spoke with are looking for a presidential candidate to fill in Trump’s "footsteps."
"I'm really open to see who can fill Trump's footsteps, not just the next person in line," one told Fox News Digital.
FOX NEWS/NORC STUDY: VOTERS LOOK TO 2028 FOCUSED ON THE ECONOMY
Sen. Chuck Schumer said President Donald Trump, seen on Oct. 28, 2026, would be the subject of Senate investigations whenever he violates the law. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"I wish Trump could run again," another said.

Another brought up the prospect of another presidential run by Gov. Ron DeSantis, R-Fla., who has tried to distance himself from the results of Tuesday’s midterms. In a news conference Wednesday, he praised Florida for keeping the state under GOP control — suggesting his governance was a reason Florida Republicans held on.
"I would like to see either JD and Marco, or JD and Gov. DeSantis," one said at the Trump rally. "That's what I would feel comfortable with. "
Beyond Vance, Rubio and DeSantis, other prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced in early 2028 discussions include Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas and Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
CRUZ-VANCE RIVALRY HEATS UP AS TEXAS SENATOR SUGGESTS VP IS 'FEELING INSECURE'
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks during a campaign rally with Republican candidate for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers in Grosse Point Woods, Mich., on Oct. 28, 2026. (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)
No major Republican contender has formally announced a 2028 presidential campaign, though the conclusion of the midterms has brought the party's next presidential nomination into sharper focus.

Despite some that Fox News Digital spoke with expressing a preference for Rubio over Vance, other Trump supporters stopped short of choosing between the two, praising both as potential successors to the president.

"I like JD Vance, and I like Marco Rubio," one said. "I think those are two very outstanding candidates that will continue to make America great again."

title: From 'Red Sprouts' to school board races, DSA's years-long effort to reach children gains momentum
summary: The DSA's "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum and "Red Sprouts" training aim to bring resistance-driven childcare and radical storytelling to young children.
story: American Parents Coalition’s Alleigh Marré warns DSA-backed efforts are embedding socialist ideology in childcare, classrooms and school boards to shape children’s worldviews as early as preschool.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is taking its message into classrooms, childcare programs and school boards, urging organizers to approach childcare "from a socialist perspective" through initiatives such as Socialist Sprouts, and it's been an initiative for years, a parental-rights watchdog warns.

In New York City, the DSA's "Red Sprouts" program held a training session in October 2026 to equip organizers to provide "resistance-driven childcare" at demonstrations, meetings and community events.
The training encouraged participants to incorporate political themes into childcare through "radical storytelling," "cooperative games" and age-appropriate discussions.

"There's been a real influx in enthusiasm and their ability and desire to recruit and grow their movement," American Parents Coalition leader Alleigh Marré told Fox News Digital. "What's particularly concerning and insidious, is their direct efforts to apply that to not just adults, but to youth."
Marré said the American Parents Coalition is working to equip parents with resources to identify and question political activism in schools, including through its "Lookout" initiative.
New York City Democratic Socialists hold a rally in Union Square on Nov. 16, 2025, to mark the start of a campaign to tax the rich and win universal childcare. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu)
PARENTS SHOULDN’T NEED THE HELP OF CONGRESS TO SEE THEIR CHILDREN’S SCHOOL CURRICULUM

The New York City DSA chapter also established Comrades With Kids, a family-focused organizing group that seeks to be a "political and social home base for working-class families." The group posted photos of DSA-themed coloring pages for children provided at a Zohran for Parents event in September 2025.
The New York initiatives are part of a larger effort by the DSA to incorporate childcare and political education into its organizing activities.

For years, the DSA's National Political Education Committee has offered training on approaching childcare for activists "from a socialist perspective," including activities for children at organizing events. In 2025, the committee outlined plans to develop a "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum geared for children, parents and caregivers involved in the movement.
The organization's efforts to introduce socialist ideas to children date back at least a decade.

In 2016, New York City DSA members launched a Socialist Sunday School for children ages 2 to 6. The program used political songs such as "Union Maid" and "Solidarity Forever," alongside children's books, including "The Lorax," to introduce discussions about corporate greed, environmentalism and organizing against unfairness.

In Ohio, the Cleveland DSA chapter created a children's coloring book to "help kids learn what we work on at DSA." Its illustrations include a version of "The Three Little Pigs" tied to the chapter's housing agenda.

Items on a table during an election night party held by the Democratic Socialists of America-LA chapter at The Greyhound on Nov. 4, 2025 in Los Angeles, Calif. (Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATIONS PUT PUBLIC SCHOOLS UNDER THE MICROSCOPE
The DSA's online store has also sold children's clothing promoting a "Green New Deal for Public Schools."

The DSA describes much of its childcare programming as a way to make political organizing more accessible to working-class families. Marré, however, argued that introducing socialist ideas to young children raises concerns about political indoctrination.

"The DSA really understands and values that if you can indoctrinate and teach these kids really young, their perceived value of, of socialism, that that's going to stick with kids for a lifetime," Marre said. "It's much easier to teach a child an idea or ideal in their infancy, and when they're very young and they're forming their worldview, and we have seen many efforts to try and capitalize on that."

"There's this really concerted effort to instill an ideology in really, really young children, rather than teaching kids how to think and introducing a breadth of ideologies of religious interests, etc.," Marré said. "It's really focused on socialist and communist aligned ideas."
Beyond its childcare programs, the DSA has also pursued a strategy to expand its influence over public education through local school board elections.

At its 2023 national convention, the DSA adopted an amendment prioritizing the recruitment and support of socialist school board candidates. Rose DuBois, one of the amendment's authors, argued that school board elections could help the organization reach "new kinds of voters, such as parents," while building the infrastructure needed to win higher-profile races.
Zohran Mamdani, mayoral candidate, during a campaign rally at United Palace in New York on Oct. 13, 2025. (Christian Monterrosa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WINS NYC HOUSE SEAT AS DSA EXPANDS ITS REACH IN CONGRESS

The Los Angeles chapter of the DSA established its own Public Education Committee, with priorities that include expanding the organization's influence on school boards, recruiting school board candidates, working with teachers unions and promoting policies such as the Green New Deal.

Those long-standing efforts come as the DSA gains political ground following the 2026 midterm elections, with DSA-backed candidates winning congressional, state legislative and local school board races.
DSA-backed positions prevailed on 23 ballot measures, including a measure in Washington where voters rejected a proposal to restore expanded parental rights in public schools.

The election results highlight the growing political reach of an organization whose members advocate shifting economic power away from private corporations and expanding government-funded programs, including universal healthcare and childcare.

The 2025 victory of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a card-carrying member of the DSA, heightened awareness of the movement's growing influence, particularly among young people. Following the 2026 midterms, three card-carrying DSA members — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, both New York Democrats — are set to represent parts of New York City in Congress.
Marré said the American Parents Coalition is working to equip parents with resources to identify and question political activism in schools, including through its "Lookout" initiative.
She warned that the impact could become more visible as newly elected DSA-backed officials take office.

"We're gonna see a lot more of the firsthand resources and the effects of this brand new class of DSA members being folded into their communities," Marré said.

title: Inside a rancher family's clash with gov't that could have ripple effect right to SCOTUS: ‘Existential threat’
summary: Wade and Teresa King say Washington's Department of Ecology fined them $267,540 over stockwater ponds the state claims are regulated wetlands.
story: King Ranch owners Wade and Teresa King and Pacific Legal Foundation senior attorney Oliver Dunford discuss their fight with the Washington State Department of Ecology over a $267,540 fine and their push for a jury trial.

The owners of a multigenerational cattle ranch say they are facing an "existential threat" after the Washington state Department of Ecology fined them hundreds of thousands of dollars over their stockwater ponds, and they are warning the case could have substantial implications nationwide.

The department fined Wade and Teresa King, owners of King Ranch in Grant and Douglas counties, $267,540 in 2023 for allegedly damaging regulated wetlands by digging ponds to provide water for their ranching operations. The Kings argue the areas, which they were ordered to restore, are long-standing stockwater ponds for their livestock, not regulated wetlands.
The Kings, who have been trying to get their case in front of a jury, told Fox News Digital that, not only is their financial stability at stake, so are the rights of other ranchers.
"Losing this fight would be an existential threat," Wade said. "I don't know how we would recover from that, to be honest with you."
HOW A LOBSTERMAN'S PRIVACY FIGHT REACHED SCOTUS — AND COULD RIPPLE FAR BEYOND THE WATER: 'AIN'T OVER YET'
King Ranch owners Wade and Teresa King are fighting the Washington state Department of Ecology over areas the state says are regulated wetlands. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)

When the Kings were first hit with the fines and restoration orders, they immediately set out to challenge them. However, the department's required process directed them to bring their case before the Pollution Control Hearings Board (PCHB), an administrative panel that does not provide jury trials.

In March, the Kings filed a separate lawsuit in Grant County Superior Court, arguing the case should not be decided by the PCHB and that doing so would violate their right to a jury trial. Months later, a judge dismissed the lawsuit, ruling the Kings first had to complete the administrative process.
The Kings appealed the decision, and a Washington Court of Appeals commissioner paused the PCHB proceedings in September while the court considers whether they are entitled to a jury trial.

"It's all under the executive branch, and they very rarely go with the property owner," Wade said, adding that Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, who was attorney general when the fight began, now has appointment authority over the board alongside the state Senate.
"They almost always side with the agencies and it's just not a fair trial for appellants like us."
The PCHB declined to comment due to the pending case.

Oliver Dunford, a senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation representing the Kings, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to petition the U.S. Supreme Court if they are unsuccessful in Washington.
HOW A SIX PACK OF BEER AND THE MAGNA CARTA COULD FINALLY FIX A PROBLEM PLAGUING AMERICANS FOR DECADES
The Kings were fined $267,540 in 2023 for allegedly damaging regulated wetlands by digging cattle ponds. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)

"We have to ask them one question: to rule that the Seventh Amendment does apply against the states, and then to argue that the Kings should have had a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment," Dunford said.
He said if the case reaches the Supreme Court, a ruling could have ripple effects across other states.

"If we prevail, it would have an enormous effect, certainly across the state of Washington, but hopefully across the country, and prevent these agencies from just issuing these fines and then essentially putting the burden on you to prove your innocence and take the case all the way to the Supreme Court just to get a chance at a jury trial," he said.

The Kings' attorneys estimate the cost of complying with the department's orders could exceed $3.7 million. But beyond the financial toll, Teresa said the orders would be "unachievable" because the areas were never wetlands in the first place.
BLUE STATE'S WATER FAILURES COULD THREATEN FOOD SUPPLIES ACROSS US, LAWMAKER WARNS
The Kings argue the areas are stockwater ponds and are fighting to have their case heard by a jury. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)
"How do we as ranchers turn these into wetlands and comply with everything that Ecology wants us to?" she said. "It'll be unachievable and it would just spin us in the ground financially."
"How are we supposed to make wetlands from non-wetlands?" Wade added.

Wade said the department has failed to give them any details on how to fix the alleged damage. He said the wetlands designation gives the department greater authority over the areas than it would if they were considered stockwater ponds.
"That's the big reason why they want to call them wetlands when they're not wetlands," Wade said.

Wade and Teresa described how the fight could also hurt their children and their children’s children. The Kings have ranched in Grant and Douglas counties since the 1950s, where Teresa said multiple generations now live and work.
TRUMP ADMIN SCRAPS ‘WEAPONIZED’ WILDLIFE RULE THAT BECAME 'BURDEN' ON AMERICAN FAMILIES AND BUSINESSES: BURGUM
The Kings say the legal battle could affect other ranchers and their constitutional rights. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)
"It’s fourth generation, then we have fifth and sixth living and working on this ranch, and we want to continue with this," she said. "We just want to be left alone."
The department said its investigation found no evidence the areas were previously stockwater ponds and accused the Kings of "damaging 23 naturally occurring wetlands" in Grant County.

"Ecology inspectors made site visits to these damaged areas where possible, but also used satellite imagery, aerial images dating from as far back as 1949, and other records to determine that the Kings had damaged 6.37 acres of naturally occurring wetlands by excavating, recontouring, and putting fill in them," the department said.

The department added it "repeatedly sought to resolve concerns about the damage" but the Kings "refused to cooperate with these efforts." They said they ordered the Kings to restore 11 more areas in Douglas County last year, bringing the total to 34, and most were on state land.
Wade said they have always protected and cared for the land that the department is now accusing them of damaging.

"We want clean water," Wade said. "Why would we pollute or cause damage to the land or the water that we rely on in our livelihood? We're generational. Why would we do something to harm ourselves that way and harm the environment?"
The Kings said the fight is far from over, with Teresa arguing the case could jeopardize exemptions other ranchers rely on to provide water for livestock.

"It's not just us," Teresa said. "We are defending every rancher in the state of Washington's exempt livestock water rights."
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: New Jersey town reveals staggering $26M theft days after election, sparking backlash
summary: Cranbury Township residents demand answers after a $26 million fraudulent wire transfer was kept secret until days after Election Day in New Jersey.
story: Residents of a New Jersey township are demanding answers after officials revealed a $26 million fraudulent wire transfer more than five weeks after the theft, just days after a local election.

A New Jersey township is facing backlash after officials revealed that $26 million was stolen in a fraudulent wire transfer, with residents questioning why the massive theft wasn't disclosed until more than five weeks later — just days after Election Day.
Cranbury Township Mayor Lisa Knierim announced Friday that the municipality had been the victim of a "sophisticated financial theft" involving approximately $26 million.
Knierim, a Democrat, said the fraudulent wire transfer took place on Sept. 28, with the funds originally designated for purchasing property to meet the township's affordable housing obligations.

A task force involving local, county, state and federal law enforcement agencies, led by the township's police department and the Middlesex County Prosecutor's Office, is working to recover the funds, according to the mayor's statement.
CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY
Cranbury Township officials disclosed a $26 million fraudulent wire transfer on Nov. 6, more than five weeks after the theft occurred and three days after Election Day. (Google Maps)
So far, investigators have frozen nearly $17.3 million in assets, leaving approximately $8.7 million outside the reported freeze.
The township said the investigation remains active, adding that additional details cannot be released.
Knierim's announcement came Nov. 6, three days after the midterm elections and more than five weeks after the theft.
Several residents responded to the announcement on the township's Facebook page, questioning the timing of the disclosure and demanding greater transparency from local officials.
NEW JERSEY MAYOR WHO CHARGED AT RESIDENT DURING COUNCIL MEETING CONCEDES ELECTION LOSS
Democrats retained control of the Cranbury Township Committee following an election held three days before officials publicly disclosed a $26 million financial theft. (Kena Betancur/Getty Images)
"I'm interested in knowing why this information was kept under wraps until after Election Day," one commenter wrote.
Another asked, "If this occurred on September 28th why is it just now being shared?"

The announcement followed Tuesday's local election, in which Democrat Thomas Szczur Jr. defeated Republican Carol Haring with 63.69% of the vote to Haring's 36.32%, according to election results published by the New Jersey secretary of state's office.
Szczur's victory preserved Democrats' control of all five seats on the Cranbury Township Committee.
The mayor acknowledged residents' concerns in her statement.
"We recognize that news of this magnitude will understandably raise questions and concerns among our residents," Knierim wrote. "Those concerns are legitimate, and we take them seriously."
NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

A New Jersey township is facing questions from residents after officials revealed that approximately $26 million intended for affordable housing-related property purchases had been stolen. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Knierim also said the township was taking steps to strengthen financial oversight and maintain municipal operations, noting that the Township Committee plans to introduce ordinances Monday to establish two new positions: assistant township administrator and assistant chief financial officer.

The committee also plans to consider hiring a municipal accounting firm for additional financial consulting support, while officials work with insurance carriers to explore potential recovery options.
It remains unclear why the township waited more than five weeks to publicly disclose the theft.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the mayor's office for additional comment.

title: Melania Trump secures $7.2M for foster care scholarships at LSU ahead of Alabama showdown
summary: Melania Trump unveiled a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at LSU for foster care youth before receiving a custom jersey and football tribute.
story: First lady Melania Trump announced scholarships in partnership with her Be Best and "Fostering the Future" initiatives Saturday at Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge.

BATON ROUGE, La. — First lady Melania Trump announced a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at Louisiana State University (LSU) on Saturday, delivering a message of hope to young Americans who have experienced foster care before receiving a special football tribute ahead of the Tigers' rivalry showdown against Alabama.

Trump wore a Dalma suede bomber jacket by Nour Hammour, paired with an Adam Lippes skirt and Manolo Blahnik BB pumps for the occasion, blending her signature polished style with a more relaxed look suited to a college football weekend.

The first lady's visit unfolded against a distinctly LSU backdrop, with purple-and-gold tailgating crowds lining the motorcade route and a massive American flag hanging above the stage inside Patrick F. Taylor Hall.
LSU cheerleaders flanked Trump during her remarks, and the Tiger mascot presented her with both scholarship checks while wearing a signature "Be Best" T-shirt.
MELANIA TRUMP CHALLENGES CONGRESS TO MAKE HER FOSTER CARE EXECUTIVE ORDER PERMANENT LAW: 'THEIR BIRTHRIGHT'

First lady Melania Trump arrives at Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport on Saturday in Baton Rouge, La., en route to Louisiana State University to an event announcing scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system as part of her "Fostering the Future" program. (Annabelle Gordon/Pool/Getty Images)
There, university officials, donors and students gathered for an announcement supporting young Americans who have experienced foster care through Trump's "Fostering the Future" initiative.
"This achievement will give young people from foster care an anchor of stability, a strong educational foundation, and a chance to build a wonderful life," Trump told attendees.
The permanent endowment includes a $5 million commitment from MMR Group, led by LSU alumnus James B. "Pepper" Rutland, and an additional $2.2 million raised from 75 LSU Foundation donors.
LSU Foundation President and CEO Krista Raney said the contributions had brought the scholarship fund to "more than $7.2 million and growing."
LSU President Wade Rousse said the $5 million leadership gift is expected to generate approximately $200,000 annually, helping students cover tuition, fees, books and room and board.
ED ORGERON-LANE KIFFIN PAIRING ALREADY PAYING DIVIDENDS FOR LSU TIGERS DURING PIVOTAL RECRUITING WEEKEND
First lady Melania Trump attends an event to announce a $5 million Fostering the Future Endowment Fund at Louisiana State University, Saturday, in Baton Rouge. (Annabelle Gordon/Pool/Getty Images)
"At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere, but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said.
The university also embraced the occasion with several football-themed gifts for the first lady.
Trump received a custom purple-and-gold LSU jersey bearing the name "MELANIA" and the number 14, along with a Tigers helmet featuring her BE BEST Fostering the Future logo.
Former LSU coach Ed Orgeron, known to fans as Coach O, joined the presentation with a specially designed commemorative football created by Big Game USA, a company owned by LSU alumnus Chris Calandra.

The initiative extended beyond the ceremony, with special patches on LSU players' jerseys, helmet decals, cheerleader uniforms, mascot attire and commemorative fan towels, according to the White House.
COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S FIRST FULL SATURDAY IS HERE AND IT'S A CELEBRATION OF AMERICA AT ITS BEST

First lady Melania Trump high-fives the LSU mascot Mike the Tiger, Saturday, in Baton Rouge, La. The first lady traveled to Louisiana to announce scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system as part of her "Fostering the Future" program. (Annabelle Gordon/Pool/Getty Images)
The celebration continued at Tiger Stadium, where the first lady's Fostering the Future initiative received special on-field recognition during LSU's highly anticipated matchup against Alabama.

Students joined LSU's Mike the Tiger mascot and others on the field for a ceremonial check presentation highlighting the $7.2 million scholarship endowment. Trump also appeared on the stadium's massive Jumbotron as fans cheered and chants of "USA" echoed through the stadium.
The game-day atmosphere included a military flyover above Tiger Stadium, adding to the spectacle as thousands of fans gathered for the SEC rivalry.
The first lady's visit extended beyond the scholarship announcement, with LSU incorporating Fostering the Future branding into players' jerseys, helmets and other game-day elements.
A special Melania Trump challenge coin was also designated for the game's opening coin toss, according to the White House.
The legendary LSU-Alabama rivalry even found its way into the scholarship announcement.
After Trump revealed that LSU has 14 Fostering the Future scholars compared with Alabama's nine, Raney offered a lighthearted observation.
"Mrs. Trump, what I heard you say is that LSU has 14 scholarship recipients and Alabama has nine," Raney said. "So I think that means we've already won the first point."
Trump told attendees that 26 universities nationwide are supporting 100 Fostering the Future scholars this semester.
"While most eyes will be on the athletes today, I encourage you to recognize LSU's Fostering the Future scholars, who are just as remarkable," she said.
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, Louisiana first lady Sharon Landry and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., were among those in attendance.
Trump also received a handcrafted wooden bowl made from a fallen limb of one of LSU's historic oak trees, a gift symbolizing the lasting impact of the scholarship initiative.
First lady Melania Trump stands with scholarship recipients at LSU as part of her "Fostering the Future" program. (Fox News Digital/Jasmine Baehr)
Fostering the Future, launched in 2021 as part of Trump's BE BEST initiative, seeks to expand educational opportunities for young people who have experienced foster care.
"A great education does more than prepare someone for work life," Trump said. "It gives something no one can ever take away."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She closed with an encouraging message to scholarship recipients.
"To the Fostering the Future scholars here today, and throughout America: I see you. I believe in you. And I will keep working to create new opportunities with you," she said.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Trump orders DOJ probe into Democrats over alleged threats against administration officials
summary: President Donald Trump accused Democrats of threatening administration officials and Republican donors and ordered the DOJ to investigate alleged "criminal" conduct.
story: Ron Johnson, R-Wis., joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss President Donald Trump's comments to Senate Republicans and a new bid for Senate minority leader.

President Donald Trump said he has ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to open an investigation into instances of Democratic lawmakers "threatening" to impeach Attorney General Todd Blanche, among others.

The announcement, which was made via a Truth Social post Saturday afternoon, came after the Democrats regained control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, winning strong majorities in both chambers of Congress.

"The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so," Trump wrote.
Since Election Day, two House Democrats — Reps. Hank Johnson, D-Ga., and Deborah Ross, D-N.C. — have publicly said they would support impeaching Blanche.
President Donald Trump asks DOJ to open investigation into Democrat lawmakers "threatening" to impeach administration officials. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images, File)
HOUSE GOP ERUPTS AT STEPHEN MILLER AS TRUMP ELEVATES HIM AFTER MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'MEGALOMANIAC'
"I personally believe that the offenses of Todd Blanche demand that he be impeached and convicted and removed from office," Johnson said Thursday in an interview on SiriusXM’s "The Dan Abrams Show."
Ross went on host Dan Abrams' radio show shortly after Johnson and said she supported impeaching Blanche as well, but she said Democrats "should start with Hegseth."

In his post, Trump denied that any "impeachable acts" had been committed by Blanche or any other administration officials. He didn't mention Johnson or Ross by name, nor did he mention the fact that Thomas Massie, R-Ky., will likely reintroduce impeachment articles against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Monday.
Trump named only one Democratic politician, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, in his post. He accused her of saying she would "go after all young people that believe in Republican Values."
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., was named by Trump in his social media post. (Tom Williams/Getty Images, File)
TRUMP CALLS OUT SENATE REPUBLICANS AFTER MIDTERM LOSSES
Trump appears to have been referring to comments Slotkin made on Oct. 13 at the University of Chicago about wanting to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" Trump.

"I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.' I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that,'" Slotkin said. "I want that deterrence message sent."
Trump also said Democrats have been threatening Republican donors "with imprisonment" because of their views.
President Donald Trump speaks on the day the final steel beam is installed in the ballroom at the White House in Washington, D.C., Wednesday. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

The president did not identify the donors that have allegedly been threatened. Democrats have, however, signaled they plan to investigate some major Republican donors and corporations when they assume control of Congress, Reuters reported this week. This could include donors to the White House ballroom.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Trump concluded his post by saying "these EXTORTIONISTS" should be imprisoned, adding that he wanted the DOJ to investigate the alleged actions as a "criminal act."
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Biden-appointed judge probes whether ICE skirted judge's release orders in Colorado cases
summary: Denver ICE Field Office Director Nathan Rasper must appear in court after 14 detainees were arrested again after court-ordered releases in Colorado.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News Digital that Biden-appointed judges are ‘almost impossible’ to work with as immigration enforcement battles intensify.

A Biden-appointed federal judge ordered ICE's Denver field office director to appear in court Monday amid concerns that immigration authorities violated judicial release orders by immediately rearresting detainees, including at least one instance outside a detention center.
Nathan Rasper has been summoned as part of an inquiry involving 14 people who were arrested after being released from immigration detention.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) maintains that ICE complied with lawful court orders and that a judicial release order does not permanently shield individuals from immigration enforcement.

"When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time," DHS said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "ICE may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage."
OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP’S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’

The Nov. 5 order issued by U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney followed an earlier ruling requiring the government to identify every case in Colorado since Oct. 27 in which ICE detained someone within 12 hours of a court-ordered release.
Federal officials subsequently identified 14 petitioners who had been arrested again after being released, but the filing did not provide the precise timing of when the rearrests occurred.
She directed officials to provide the exact dates and times of those releases and rearrests and identify any additional individuals immediately detained following court-ordered releases.

A man holds his immigration paperwork while handcuffed after being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents outside an immigration courtroom June 17, 2025, at the Jacob K. Javits federal building in New York. (AP)

The additional reporting requirements followed a Nov. 4 hearing at which Sweeney questioned whether ICE was circumventing judicial orders by briefly releasing detainees before immediately taking them back into custody. At that hearing, she ordered Rasper to appear at a follow-up hearing Monday to address the agency's practices.

The inquiry stems in part from the case of Ramon Quintero Alvarez, who was released from immigration detention Oct. 27 before ICE immediately took him back into custody, according to a government court filing.
In a Nov. 3 court filing, federal government attorneys said they would not submit a legal brief defending the lawfulness of Alvarez's continued detention.
The immigrant detention center operated by the privately-owned GEO Group for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Aurora, Colo. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The filing prompted Sweeney to convene the Nov. 4 hearing at which Assistant U.S. attorneys Andrew Soler and Kevin Traskos appeared alongside ICE Assistant Field Office Director Nichole Black, who testified under oath about the circumstances surrounding Alvarez's rearrest.
APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS

At a Nov. 4 hearing, Sweeney ordered Alvarez released and barred immigration authorities from detaining him again unless the government demonstrated, by clear and convincing evidence at a bond hearing, that he posed a flight risk or danger to the community.

The government must submit the additional information requested by Sweeney by 8 a.m. Monday, ahead of Rasper's scheduled court appearance later that morning. The proceedings could shed light on ICE's compliance with judicial release orders, but Sweeney has not indicated whether she intends to pursue contempt proceedings.
An agent escorts a person in custody. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The dispute comes as ICE faces similar legal challenges across Colorado, where other Biden-appointed federal judges, including U.S. District Judges Nina Wang and S. Kato Crews, have presided over cases involving disputes over immigration detention and court-ordered releases.

Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado for comment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Newsom’s death row commutations spark DA revolt; prosecutors warn of legal fight
summary: California district attorneys accused Gavin Newsom of overriding juries and ignoring victims' families with his plan to commute all 548 death sentences in the state.
story: Former DOJ prosecutor Jim Trusty reacts to Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute hundreds of death sentences, criticism from victims' families and questions about the decision's timing. He also weighs in on the federal investigations into Rep. Ilhan Omar's fraud allegations.

At least a dozen California district attorneys are publicly condemning Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute all 548 death sentences in the state, arguing the sweeping move overrides juries, disregards victims’ families and defies the will of state voters.

Newsom announced the plan Thursday, saying state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values. The move would convert the sentences to life without parole, though 382 cases still require approval from at least four California Supreme Court justices, according to The Associated Press.

In response, prosecuting attorneys across California have raised concerns about victims’ rights, the governor’s constitutional authority and the role of the California Supreme Court in reviewing hundreds of the commutations.
"Justice requires case-by-case consideration, not one-size-fits-all decisions," Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho said in response to Newsom's action.
THREE STATES CARRY OUT EXECUTIONS ON SAME DAY AMID RENEWED DEATH PENALTY DEBATE
A table fitted with restraints holds down death row prisoners while they are given a lethal injection at Huntsville Unit (Walls Unit) in Huntsville, Texas. (Greg Smith/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images)
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer described the move as "mercy for the wolves" that inflicts "the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep."

Spitzer noted that regulations implemented by California’s Board of Parole Hearings on Oct. 1 allow thousands of prisoners serving life without parole to become eligible for parole, arguing that Newsom's latest death row commutations could put these inmates "one step closer" to release. Newsom’s office says, however, that the affected prisoners will remain in prison and are not eligible for release.

"The governor is attempting to appear courageous with this decision. He is not courageous. His commutations are solely based upon power and political aspirations," added San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson, who accused Newsom of caring more about politics than people.
"Courage would require speaking with crime victims and the surviving family members of the people murdered by these death row inmates."
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM
Anderson cited the case of Kevin Cooper, a California death row inmate convicted of killing Josh Ryen’s parents and sister and Ryen’s friend, Chris Hughes, and leaving Ryen for dead.
Anderson said Newsom did not contact Ryen or Hughes’ mother, Mary Ann Hughes, to ask their views on a possible commutation, and Ryen has never received a call from the governor.

"Courage would require the governor to follow Marsy’s Law, California’s constitutional rights belonging to victims of crime," Anderson continued. "He has not. I am not aware of any victims’ family members receiving notice of these commutations from the governor."

Anderson and several other California prosecutors who spoke out against Newsom's death row commutations also framed the dispute as a challenge to the jury system and an override of the will of California voters.

They said jurors in each case heard the evidence, weighed all the necessary factors and decided whether death was warranted, with judges and appellate courts later reviewing those verdicts. Newsom’s blanket action, they argue, substitutes one statewide decision for hundreds of individualized judgments.
NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson answers questions during a news conference outside the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department in Rancho Cucamonga April 10, 2026. (Anjali Sharif-Paul, The Sun/SCNG)
"A single order commuting all of them would set aside hundreds of individualized judgments without examining the facts of even one," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow said.

"It invalidates the exhausting, emotionally wrenching work of our citizens who sat on juries, weighed horrific evidence and delivered lawful verdicts. Most unforgivably, it is a slap in the face to victims and their families," said San Joaquin District Attorney Ron Freitas.
"This decision does not bind wounds; it tears them wide open all over again."

The prosecutors pointed out that California voters rejected death penalty repeal initiatives in 2012 and 2016, while approving Proposition 66 in 2016, which changed procedures for challenging death sentences and was promoted by supporters as a way to speed up the process. The district attorneys argued Newsom’s blanket action overrides those ballot-box decisions without repealing the law.

"A blanket commutation is a mass erasure of justice. It overrides the will of California voters who have repeatedly defended capital punishment at the ballot box," Freitas added in his response to Newsom's action.
A prison is shown in an undated file photo as California district attorneys condemn Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute all 548 state death sentences. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Some California prosecutors who spoke out against Newsom's controversial move signaled that the dispute may not end with public statements.

San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan said her office was "researching any lawful remedies" that would allow victims’ voices to be heard and considered, while Kern County District Attorney Cynthia Zimmer was more direct, saying, "This assault on justice will be challenged."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman acknowledged that commuting existing sentences falls within the governor’s constitutional authority, but said, "That power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty. Only the Legislature or the voters can do that."
Newsom’s clemency announcement clarifies that it "does not repeal the death penalty" and is limited to commuting California’s current death sentences.
Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Republican state lawmakers reported Omar to the IRS in 2019
summary: Years before Omar's latest federal probe, Minnesota Republicans flagged her controversial tax filings to the IRS, according to newly obtained correspondence.
story: Chad Pergram reports on Capitol Hill regarding the reopened investigation into Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2009 marriage to Ahmed Elmi.

EXCLUSIVE: A group of Minnesota Republican state lawmakers asked the IRS in August 2019 to "conduct a detailed reexamination" of tax filings by Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., based on a report from a state board suggesting she filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 with a man she was not legally married to, according to a letter obtained by Fox News Digital.

The letter was sent after the Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board issued a report June 6, 2019, indicating Omar had filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 with Ahmed Hirsi despite being legally married to another man, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, at the time.
The joint tax returns came up during the Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board’s examination of a $1,500 expense associated with Omar’s campaign committee.

The board was investigating whether the expenditure was a legitimate campaign-related expense or whether campaign funds had been used to pay for services that benefited Omar personally. The payment was part of a larger $2,250 reimbursement to the Kjellberg Law Office for legal and other services.
In 2019, a group of Minnesota Republican state lawmakers asked the IRS to investigate tax filings by Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (Adam Gray/AP Photo)
ILHAN OMAR ISSUES STUNNING ADMISSION WHEN CONFRONTED WITH BROTHER MARRIAGE RUMORS

In response to the board’s questions, Omar’s campaign committee explained that the Kjellberg Law Office had retained the accounting firm Frederick & Rosen to obtain and review financial records as part of the campaign committee’s efforts to respond to allegations about Omar’s marital history.

According to the committee’s explanation, Frederick & Rosen prepared releases for Omar and Ahmed Hirsi to sign, so the firm could obtain copies of their filed joint federal income tax returns for 2014 and 2015 from the IRS.
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., continues to generate headlines related to her finances. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
The board concluded that the committee had not demonstrated that the $1,500 expense benefited the campaign and required Omar to reimburse the committee.
JD VANCE SAYS DOJ LOOKING INTO IF ILHAN OMAR COMMITTED IMMIGRATION FRAUD AMID BROTHER-MARRIAGE ALLEGATIONS

Omar married Hirsi in 2002 in their Muslim faith tradition, and they ended their relationship in that tradition in 2008, Newsweek reported. She then legally married Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in February 2009, according to public records, as reported by Newsweek.
According to divorce documents obtained by Fox News Digital, Omar legally divorced Elmi in December 2017.

Carla Kjellberg, a lawyer for Omar and her campaign committee, stated during the board proceedings that Frederick & Rosen’s services provided "some personal benefit to Rep. Omar," because "there was an issue with her tax returns that needed to be corrected regardless of her status as a candidate," according to the board’s report.
In a letter to then-IRS Commissioner Charles Rettig dated Aug. 6, 2019, the state lawmakers asked the IRS to undertake a review in light of the Minnesota Campaign Finance Board report.

"Due to recent developments, I believe probable cause exists for an investigation into Rep. Omar's tax filings," the letter, signed by Minnesota state Reps. Steve Drazkowski, Linda Runbeck, Glenn Gruenhagen, Shane Mekeland, John Poston, Eric Lucero, Duane Quam, Tim Miller, Cal Bahr and Jeremy Munson, said.
Drazkowski told Fox News Digital the IRS never responded to the request.
The IRS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Fox News Digital could not confirm whether the IRS followed through with the lawmakers’ request.

Federal tax confidentiality rules generally restrict what the agency can disclose about individual taxpayers. The Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board issued its findings on June 6, 2019, after two complaints filed by Drazkowski.

Although the board required Omar to repay the $1,500 that her campaign had paid the Kjellberg Law Firm for Frederick & Rosen’s services related to the tax returns, it rejected the allegation that this money was payment for Omar’s personal divorce proceeding, in which Kjellberg also represented her.
The board also required Omar to repay campaign funds used for certain travel expenses, including trips to Boston, New York and Washington, D.C.

After the board's 2019 findings, Omar said she was "glad" the process was complete and welcomed the board's determination regarding allegations that she had improperly used campaign funds for personal expenses. However, she did not address the portion of the board’s report concerning the joint tax returns she submitted with Hirsi.
Omar did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

In a separate letter obtained by Fox News Digital, the Republican state lawmakers, led by Drazkowski, asked Cynthia Bauerly, then the commissioner of the Minnesota Department of Revenue, in August 2019 to review Omar's joint tax filings.
Drazkowski said neither Bauerly nor the Minnesota Department of Revenue responded to the lawmakers' request.
The Minnesota Department of Revenue did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The letter from the lawmakers urging the state and federal tax reporting agencies to investigate Omar’s joint tax filings came two months after Drazkowski urged Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., to refer his concerns about Omar's tax filings to the House Ethics Committee.

As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Craig told Drazkowski in a letter he could submit information himself to the Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), which was renamed to the Office of Congressional Conduct in 2021.
Ilhan Omar with Ahmed Hirsi in 2018. (Kerem Yucel/AFP via Getty Images)

The congressional ethics process allows members of the public and lawmakers to submit information concerning alleged misconduct, although the independent ethics office and the House Committee on Ethics have separate procedures.

In late October, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News the federal investigation into Omar regarding potential immigration and marriage fraud had been referred to the Department of Justice as a "large case" that targets multiple individuals rather than just one person.
The DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on whether the investigation is looking into the 2014 and 2015 joint tax filings flagged by the state lawmakers in 2019.

title: California prosecutors slam Newsom's death row commutations, accuse governor of putting 'politics over people'
summary: District attorneys and law enforcement unions blasted Gov. Gavin Newsom's mass commutation of 548 death row sentences as a betrayal of victims' families.
story: San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow accused Gov. Gavin Newsom of ignoring crime victims and violating the will of California voters following a sweeping announcement on death row commutations.

District attorneys and law enforcement unions across California have publicly condemned Gov. Gavin Newsom following his announcement to commute the sentences of 548 death row inmates, a decision one prosecutor called a slap in the face to victims' families.
Newsom’s sweeping order to commute the condemned inmates to life in prison without the possibility of parole has drawn intense criticism alongside praise from anti-death penalty advocates.
"I think it's all about politics, sadly. Politics is over people in this case, and that's a real sad state of affairs," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow told Fox News Digital.
ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION

Law enforcement officials and prosecutors have criticized Gov. Gavin Newsom for issuing a blanket commutation for all of California's death row inmates. (Jane Tyska/Digital First Media/East Bay Times via Getty Images/Frazer Harrison/WireImage)
In an open letter detailing his decision, Newsom said California's capital punishment system is fundamentally at odds with the state's principles.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom wrote. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."
POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION
Upon taking office in 2019, Newsom issued an executive moratorium on capital punishment. California has not carried out an execution since 2006.
The backlash to the governor's announcement was immediate.
FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD
"Justice will not have been served for these victims, dozens of them in San Diego County," said Lt. Jared Wilson, president of the San Diego Police Officers Association.
"Their last memories were of these evil, evil men who took their lives. What Gavin Newsom has done is awful."

Lt. Sam Robinson calls to open a door at San Quentin State Prison's death row in San Quentin, Calif., Aug. 15, 2016. The prison is California's oldest penitentiary and houses the state's only death row for men with 700 condemned inmates. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Wilson and other law enforcement officials strongly criticized the blanket clemency, citing cases like that of Jesse Michael Gomez, who was sentenced to death for the 2016 murder of San Diego police officer Jonathan "J.D." De Guzman.

"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty, and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," said Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman.
"Until the law is changed, my office will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand."
NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer called the commutations "mercy for the wolves … while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep," saying voters in California have upheld the death penalty in recent years.
Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, who previously ran for governor, noted that 127 inmates on California’s death row were sentenced for crimes committed in his county.
"These sentences were not handed down without due process," he said. "They followed extensive investigations, lengthy trials, evidence presented in court and decisions made by juries and judges.

"Yet, with one sweeping executive decision, the governor has chosen to override those outcomes, disregarding the voices of victims’ families, the work of prosecutors and the pursuit of justice that took years to achieve."
College students Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford were killed separately. Their killer, Rex Krebs, was sentenced to death for the brutal slayings. (San Luis Obispo County District Attorney)

Among the 548 inmates whose sentences were commuted are two men convicted in San Luis Obispo County: Michael Whisenhunt, 61, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of his girlfriend's 1-year-old daughter, Kesha Gurke; and Rex Krebs, 60, who was convicted in the brutal slayings of two female college students.
CHARLES MANSON CULT FOLLOWER BRUCE DAVIS, CONVICTED IN TWO 1969 KILLINGS, DIES BEHIND BARS AT 83
Dow noted that families of the victims were neither consulted nor notified prior to Newsom's public announcement.
"I was just sickened, frankly, for the crime victims in California who were slapped in the face by our governor," Dow said.
JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA'S NITROGEN GAS EXECUTION METHOD, RULES IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY CRUEL
Addressing arguments from anti-death penalty groups who contend that capital punishment is inherently flawed and racially biased, Dow defended the current legal framework.
