title: Two experienced skydivers die after midair collision entangles their parachutes
summary: The two skydivers collided midair at about 150 feet during an organized skydive in Southern California, entangling their parachutes.
story: First responders and investigators work at the scene after a skydiving plane crashed moments after takeoff in northeastern France, killing all 11 people aboard. (Reuters)
Two experienced skydivers died Friday when their parachutes became entangled during an organized dive in Southern California.

Georgia Jean, 56, of Box Elder, S.D., and Levi Pimentel, 29, of Aurora, Ill., both licensed skydivers, began to plummet at about 150 feet above the ground when they collided midair at Skydive Elsinore around noon in Lake Elsinore, about 75 miles southeast of Los Angeles.
The freefall portion of the skydive was normal, as was the opening of the parachutes, Skydive Elsinore said.
FRENCH INVESTIGATORS PROBE FATAL SKYDIVING PLANE CRASH THAT KILLED PILOT AND 10 PARACHUTISTS
A file photo of a person skydiving. (Skydive Dubai/Getty Images)
Jean and Pimentel suffered "traumatic injuries" and were rushed by ambulance to a hospital, the Riverside County Fire Department said on social media.
They were pronounced dead at the hospital.
MISSOURI SKYDIVING PLANE CRASH THAT KILLED ALL 12 ABOARD IS A 'DAVASTATING LOSS,' COMPANY SAYS
Skydive Elsinore is located in Lake Elsinore. (Glenn Koenig/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
"The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground," Skydive Elsinore said in a statement.
Pimentel was a lead skydiving instructor at iFLY Naperville in Illinois, according to her LinkedIn, and Jean had done more than 1,700 jumps, according to her website.
Two U.S. Army skydivers perform a stunt during an air show in Southern California. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Ex-police officer accused of stabbing NYC jogger to death appears emotionless in new photos
summary: Sayed Mohassib was seen led away in handcuffs after being charged with second-degree murder in the stabbing death of Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez.
story: Sayed Mohassib was escorted Saturday from a Brooklyn police precinct. (WNYW)
An ex-NYPD police officer accused of murdering a Brooklyn jogger was seen being led out of the 62nd Precinct police station in handcuffs on Saturday.
Sayed Mohassib has been charged with second-degree murder in the stabbing Oct. 30 death of Katie Suarez at the Shore Parkway Greenway.
He is also charged with tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.
Mohassib, who wore a red Van Dutch jacket, black top and jeans, showed little emotion as he was escorted by police.
NYC WOMAN CRITICALLY INJURED AFTER BEING STABBED MULTIPLE TIMES WHILE JOGGING ALONG BROOKLYN WATERFRONT
Sayed Mohassib showed little emotion as he was escorted away in handcuffs. (WNYW)
He told police that he woke up covered in blood with no memory of the attack, adding that he threw the knife in the garbage, according to the New York Post.
Sayed Mohassib is seen after his arrest. (WNYW)
Suarez, 28, was running along a waterfront path around 8 p.m. when she was stabbed in her neck.
She had been on the phone with her parents before the attack and when they got cut off, they went looking for her along the path where they found her in critical condition.
She died of her injuries at the hospital.
COPS RETURN TO NEW JERSEY MOTHER'S HOME MONTHS AFTER SHE WAS FOUND STABBED AND HUSBAND CALLED 911
The NYPD says Katie Suarez, 28, was stabbed in the neck several times in an unprovoked attack that happened as she was on a run in Brooklyn on a popular jogging and biking path. (NYPD; Google Maps)
Mohassib briefly served with the NYPD before he left for the Marines, where he was deemed unfit for service, the Post reported.
The 27-year-old was most recently working as a public school aide.
The New York City Department of Education told FOX 5 that Mohassib has been suspended and will be fired depending on a conviction.

"We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed," the department said.
Police have not released a motive or said if Mohassib had any relationship to Suarez.

title: Turning Point USA event at University of New Mexico ends with two arrests and a string of charges
summary: Video shows two men allegedly plotting to hurl objects at a Turning Point USA campus event at the University of New Mexico before their arrest.
story: A 70-year-old man was arrested in New Hampshire after allegedly slapping Turning Point USA volunteer Rainer Vesey at a polling place. Vesey and his brother, Asher Vesey, who recorded the incident, recount the confrontation.
Two men were arrested Monday at the University of New Mexico for allegedly plotting to hurl objects at attendees of a Turning Point USA event.
Kevin Castro and Harrison Magnus were arrested Monday by the University of New Mexico Police Department after attending a Turning Point USA event on campus, according to KRQE.
While court documents didn't name the event, the university's TPUSA chapter hosted a Prove Me Wrong event that day featuring Students for Life of America President Kristan Hawkins.
Video posted online by the Turning Point USA chapter shows Magnus appearing to yell at the crowd as he's being taken away by police officers who placed him in handcuffs.
UTAH STUDENT CITED AFTER PHYSICAL ALTERCATION WITH COLLEGE REPUBLICAN CAUGHT ON CAMERA
Harrison Magnus was arrested on charges of conspiracy, disorderly conduct and concealing identity, according to KRQE. (MDC)

Castro allegedly hurled a lacrosse ball toward the crowd, nearly striking someone, according to court documents. He was arrested on charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, disorderly conduct, and conspiracy.
Magnus was allegedly talking to Castro regarding plans to throw objects into the crowd and was arrested on charges of conspiracy, disorderly conduct and concealing identity.
A University of New Mexico spokesman confirmed the arrests to Fox News Digital and said the school supports free expression but won't tolerate violence or unlawful behavior on campus.

"UNM remains committed to providing a safe, healthy and inclusive environment for all who learn, work and live on our campuses," the spokesman said. "The university upholds freedom of expression and will not tolerate threats, violence or other conduct that violates the law or university policies."
Fox News Digital reached out to an attorney for Magnus. It was not immediately clear if Castro had an attorney.

title: 9 mystery fingerprints from OJ Simpson murder case could hold new clues more than 30 years later
summary: Nine unidentified fingerprints from the Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman crime scene could now be retested using modern forensic technology.
story: 'Outnumbered' reacts to a report linking criminal informant Joey Ippolito to the O.J. Simpson murder case. His brother claims Joey had bloody hands on the night of the murders and may have helped Simpson.

Nine fingerprints that went unidentified during the original O.J. Simpson murder investigation could hold new clues more than 30 years later, and one filmmaker believes advances in forensic technology could help reveal who left them behind.
Ari Mark co-directed the Peacock docuseries, "OJ's Accomplice," which reexamines the 1994 murders of Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ron Goldman.

The series explores the theory that the former NFL star may not have acted alone, focusing on convicted drug trafficker and Simpson associate Joey Ippolito, who reportedly had ties to organized crime.

Mark told Fox News Digital he wants investigators to consider reexamining nine fingerprints recovered from the crime scene that could not be matched to any known samples during the original investigation.
NICOLE BROWN SIMPSON TOLD FORMER LOVER SHE'D 'RATHER DIE' THAN RETURN TO OJ SIMPSON BEFORE HER MURDER
O.J. Simpson sits in Superior Court in Los Angeles in 1994 during an open court session. "OJ's Accomplice" is currently available for streaming. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"The fact that there's nine fingerprints sitting around that nobody wants to put through a system that's very updated and technologically not what it was before, that just seems unnecessary," Mark said. "Just do it.

"You can take latent prints and analyze those in a way that you couldn't before," Mark continued. "Also, remember, the systems over time are obviously collecting more data and more people. So, if you're looking for a match, you have a greater chance of getting one all these years later."
Former DEA agent Robert Brisolari appears in Peacock’s "OJ’s Accomplice," which explores the theory that O.J. Simpson may not have acted alone. (Peacock)

In 1995, the Los Angeles Times reported that none of the identifiable fingerprints investigators collected at the Bundy Drive condominium where Brown Simpson and Goldman were murdered matched Simpson. Fingerprint specialist Gilbert Aguilar, a defense witness, testified that police knew that Simpson's fingerprints did not match the identifiable prints recovered at the crime scene.
O.J. Simpson and Nicole Brown Simpson March 16, 1994, in Los Angeles. She was murdered in June of that year. (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

Under questioning by lead defense attorney Johnnie Cochran Jr., Aguilar testified that nine prints found at Bundy Drive could not be matched to any known sample. According to the Los Angeles Times, Simpson's lawyers argued that unknown attackers committed the murders and that detectives failed to adequately investigate that possibility because they quickly concluded Simpson had killed his ex-wife and her friend.
WATCH: Kato Kaelin describes OJ Simpson encounter that raised suspicions

According to Aguilar's testimony, investigators compared the unidentified prints with those of Simpson, Brown Simpson and 58 friends, relatives and acquaintances but found no matches. Aguilar also testified that investigators searched federal and state computerized fingerprint databases without finding a match.
Mark said his goal for the docuseries was "to raise enough questions that it gets a second look."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
A family photo of Ronald Goldman, who was murdered with O.J. Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, June 12, 1994. (Lee Celano/WireImage)

"I'm very careful about the call to action because there are victims' families involved here, and you would want them to be supportive of that," Mark said. "That would be my first priority. Assuming it was something they were interested in, I think everyone deserves to know what actually happened and if that involves a second person, third person or whatever it is, great."
Aguilar, who appears in the docuseries, raised the possibility that today's expanded fingerprint databases could produce a match.
WATCH: Alan Dershowitz calls for independent OJ Simpson probe over lingering third-party questions
"At the crime scene, there were nine identifiable prints that I never identified to whom they belong," Aguilar said in the documentary.

"Back in 1994, you're running prints through AFIS (Automated Fingerprint Identification System). But, first, it's checking everybody that's been arrested by the Los Angeles Police Department. Then it would be run through Sacramento. Then run through all the Western states.

Denise Brown, sister of murder victim Nicole Brown Simpson, cries on the witness stand in Los Angeles as a picture she took of an injured Nicole Brown Simpson is shown on a screen. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"If somebody is arrested outside your database, like in New York or the state of Florida, you’re not going to get anything," Aguilar continued. "LAPD has all the prints, and they could have them [tested again]. They may or may not. I don’t know. It’s up to them now."
It is unclear whether investigators have reexamined the nine unidentified fingerprints using modern forensic technology or updated fingerprint databases.
Tom Lange is a retired LAPD detective who served as one of the lead investigators in the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman. (Peacock)
An LAPD spokesperson told Fox News Digital the investigation remains open.

O.J. Simpson looks at a new pair of Aris extra-large gloves prosecutors had him put on for the jury during his double murder trial in Los Angeles June 21, 1995. The gloves were the same type found at the Bundy murder scene and the Simpson estate. (AFP via Getty Images)

"The O.J. Simpson case remains an open and ongoing investigation. The Department has an obligation to continue to pursue justice in this matter, at a point that, if new evidence is found, detectives will follow those investigatory leads. At this point there is no other information available for release."
In the docuseries, defense investigator Pat McKenna said the fingerprints should easily be sent to a lab for further analysis.
Kato Kaelin was staying in a guesthouse at O.J. Simpson’s estate on the night of the 1994 murders and later testified at Simpson’s criminal trial. (Peacock)
"This is like a door," he said. "Wide open. Don't you want to close that door? I would think they should want to do that. But I think they're afraid of what it would show."
Pat McKenna, an investigator for O.J. Simpson’s defense team during his 1995 murder trial, appears in the Peacock docuseries, "OJ’s Accomplice." (Peacock)

According to the docuseries, the producers asked the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office to have the unidentified fingerprints reexamined but received no response. Fox News Digital contacted the office for comment.

"I wouldn't put anything past technology," Mark said. "I think we all know that tech, it's just gotten so advanced, especially when it comes to forensics, that I believe something could be pulled from those fingerprints. Ideally, there'd be some sort of DNA that's been preserved, and the right type of reopening would force a reinvestigation of those materials.
OJ Simpson in a Los Angeles Police Department mugshot (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)
"I feel very confident that if everyone was on the same page, and we wanted to look at something objectively and see if there's any new truth there, we could do it."
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
OJ Simpson, Nicole Brown Simpson and their two children attend the "Naked Gun 33 1/3" premiere at the Paramount Pictures Studio Backlot in Hollywood. (Barry King/WireImage)
The unidentified fingerprints are part of the docuseries' broader investigation into whether Simpson had an accomplice the night Brown Simpson and Goldman were killed.

Before the docuseries premiered, Joey Ippolito's brother, Sam Ippolito, told The New York Times Joey returned to a Los Angeles apartment around midnight on June 12, 1994, carrying a bag containing a heavy object.
Police officers stand outside the home of Nicole Brown Simpson in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles in June 1994. (Getty Images)

Sam said his brother appeared to have blood on his hands after leaving the apartment hours earlier to help a friend. According to Sam, Joey stuffed his clothes into the bag and instructed him to dispose of it while he showered.
Sam Ippolito told the newspaper he tossed the bag into a dumpster near a construction site along Doheny Drive in Los Angeles. Sam shared a similar account in the docuseries.
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

Sam Ippolito (pictured here), the brother of Joseph "Joey" Ippolito, has alleged that his brother returned to their Los Angeles apartment on the night of the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman and asked him to dispose of a bag containing a heavy object. Sam later sought to retract his account. (Peacock)

Sam's account has also faced questions about its credibility. According to The New York Times, he sought compensation from the newspaper and later attempted to retract his statements after the newspaper declined his request for payment. Friends and relatives have disputed suggestions that Ippolito participated in the murders.

Ippolito, who escaped from a Florida prison in May 1994, became a federal informant after his arrest in August 1995, while Simpson's nationally televised murder trial was nearing its conclusion. He died in 2006.
Ron Goldman's father, Fred Goldman, and his sister, Kim Goldman, in court. (Getty Images)

A December 1996 federal prosecution memorandum, unsealed at The New York Times' request, described Ippolito as a valuable source who possessed information about Simpson's alleged efforts to dispose of the murder weapon and his attempted flight from authorities.

Charles "Charlie" Ehrlich, a longtime friend of O.J. Simpson who later became his co-defendant in the 2007 Las Vegas armed robbery case, appears in Peacock’s "OJ’s Accomplice." (Peacock)

Former federal prosecutor David Kelley described Ippolito in the memorandum as a "remarkable source of information" whose cooperation had proven valuable to investigators. Kelley later told The New York Times he did not believe Ippolito participated in the murders.
"My instinct is that not only did I feel that he was telling the truth, but I also felt that he had more to share," Mark said.
Prosecutor Marcia Clark points to a chart as she describes to jurors where evidence was found at O.J. Simpson's home during opening statements in the murder trial. (AFP via Getty Images)
"I think The New York Times probably spooked him a bit because they are a big publication. … But I really do believe him. I believed him then, I believe him now."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Tanya Brown, the youngest sister of Nicole Brown Simpson, has become an advocate for domestic violence awareness following her sister’s 1994 murder. (Peacock)
Brown Simpson's sister, Tanya Brown, rejects the theory that Simpson had an accomplice. In the docuseries, Tanya Brown said she believes Simpson alone was responsible for her sister's murder.

"I think it's impossible if you're in her position to speculate about theories, and I don't blame her for that," Mark said. "Everything about her felt like the little sister of somebody who's an unfortunate victim."
Nicole Brown Simpson's grave  (Sygma via Getty Images)
Simpson and Brown Simpson married in 1985. They had two children, Sydney and Justin, and divorced in 1992. Two years later, Brown Simpson and Goldman were found stabbed to death.
SEND US A TIP
The white Ford Bronco, driven by Al Cowlings and carrying O.J. Simpson, during a 90-minute slow-speed car chase on June 17, 1994, on the 405 freeway in Los Angeles. (Sygma via Getty Images)

Investigators quickly focused on Simpson. After the 1995 murder trial, he was acquitted of killing Brown Simpson and Goldman. In 1997, a civil jury found Simpson liable for their deaths. He later served nearly nine years in prison after his conviction on armed robbery and other charges stemming from an unrelated incident in Las Vegas. He died in April 2024 at age 76.

OJ Simpson died April 10, 2024, at age 76. He had been battling prostate cancer. (Jason Bean-Pool/Getty Images)

title: Navy veteran blindsided as attacker could land parole hearing months after sentencing: ‘Where is my justice?’
summary: Amy's 1992 Valentine's Day rape cold case was solved by DNA evidence, but a VINE text revealed Virginia's parole board may review her attacker.
story: A Virginia rape survivor received a VINE text that the parole board may review her attacker's case months after DNA evidence solved her 1992 cold case and Anthony Favors was sentenced.
For 33 years, Amy has lived with the trauma of a 1992 Valentine's Day rape in Virginia, a cold case that finally cracked last year when DNA evidence linked the crime to a convicted rapist.

In September 2025, Anthony Favors, 57, who initially faced six indictments, including abduction and burglary, took a plea deal for two counts of rape to secure a 24-year prison sentence. Norfolk Judge Everett A. Martin Jr. ordered 12 years for each count to run consecutively.
Months later, Amy received an automated VINE text that Virginia’s parole board planned to review Favors’ case for possible release.
"I finally get some sort of closure and justice. And then I get a text," Amy told Fox News Digital. "Nobody yet has told me how he's even eligible for parole."
Amy was sexually assaulted by Anthony Favors while she was in the Navy. (Courtesy of Amy)
SUSAN SMITH ELIGIBLE FOR PAROLE AGAIN AFTER BEING DENIED RELEASE FOR DROWNING HER 2 SONS IN 1994
Norfolk Commonwealth’s Attorney Ramin Fatehi confirmed to Fox News Digital that Favors will likely have a "discretionary parole hearing" within the next few months.

Fatehi explained that a bureaucratic overlap triggered the hearing. The parole board previously considered Favors for release on a previous rape conviction but never granted it, legally opening the door for the upcoming review.
"It’s discretionary because he had been locked up for so long. He is theoretically eligible," Fatehi said.
FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS
Separate rape case

Favors was serving a 60-year sentence for a separate March 1992 rape when a 2024 DNA hit linked him to Amy’s case. Since he committed his offenses before Jan. 1, 1995, Virginia's old sentencing laws authorized the Virginia Parole Board to consider him for release.
Anthony Favors was sentenced to 24 years in prison for raping a woman in 1992. (Virginia State Police)
Fatehi said there is a "slim chance to zero" of actually releasing Favors, but the possibility of an impending hearing left Amy reeling.
MAX FACTOR HEIR'S FORMER LAWYER DETAILS JUDGE'S ERROR THAT WIPED OUT 124-YEAR RAPE SENTENCE
"The only word I can think of right now, honestly, is disgusting," she said. "It's wrong. How can you do that? Where is my justice?"

The attack altered the course of Amy's life. Favors beat and assaulted the active-duty Navy sailor for hours at her Norfolk apartment. Despite the trauma, she reported directly to her shift on a Navy ship immediately after the attack.
SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED

Decades later, the psychological scars have dictated her daily routine. She battles severe PTSD, chronic sleep deprivation and hypervigilance that forces her to constantly check and recheck her door locks.
Amy was raped in Virginia while she was in the Navy. (Courtesy of Amy)

"Some of the things that I did that I thought were normal were not normal. And I still do," Amy said. "Check the locks, recheck the locks, check the locks, recheck the locks. I'm not sleeping again because ... it's the unknown.
CONVICTED PREDATORS FACE LIFETIME BARRIER UNDER GOP LAWMAKER’S SWEEPING VICTIM PROTECTION BILL
"If you took the Amy before my rape and the Amy after my rape, I am two different people."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Heather Keeley, director of the nonprofit advocacy group Stand Tall, said survivors already carry the weight of their past assaults. By granting Favors a future parole hearing, she argued, the justice system actively expands that trauma by forcing victims to endlessly relive it.
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM
"He was sentenced to 24 years in prison, which wouldn't even put him up for parole 12 years later," Keeley told Fox News Digital.
"And here it is, less than six months later, and she's calling us all that she just received a text message that he's going before a parole board. ... How is that even possible?"

Reliving a nightmare

She plans to ask the parole board for a three-year deferral, so the state does not force her to relive the attack annually.

"I now have to explain myself again as to why he shouldn't get out. ... It's too much. But I gotta speak for me, and I gotta speak for these other victims who can't speak for themselves. So, I gotta do it."

title: Newsom orders California’s most reviled killers off death row: 10 of the worst who could benefit
summary: Gavin Newsom's death row commutation covers 548 inmates on California's death row, including notorious serial killers like Randy Kraft and Chester Turner.
story: Former DOJ prosecutor Jim Trusty discusses Gov. Gavin Newsom's decision to commute California death row sentences and the investigations into Rep. Ilhan Omar on 'America's Newsroom.'
Thanks to a Nov. 5 action by California Gov. Gavin Newsom, 548 inmates on the state's death row will have their sentences commuted to life in prison as he moves to clear death row.
"I have decided to commute every death sentence," Newsom wrote in an open letter, acknowledging that he understood that the decision would anger people and hurt the victims' families who oppose it.

"I will therefore issue the same commutation to every condemned person — life without the possibility of parole, the most severe punishment I can lawfully impose and the state of California can ethically enforce," he added.
MICHAEL RUIZ: CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS REVOLT AFTER NEWSOM ORDERS STATE'S WORST KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW
California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during an event held by the state Democratic Party at the Clubhouse at King's Grant in Summerville, S.C., Sept. 3, 2026.  (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)

Newsom’s announcement doesn’t automatically remove every inmate from death row. State law would require the Supreme Court’s approval to commute sentences for inmates with numerous felony convictions. This includes hundreds of inmates currently on death row.
Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.
California is home to some of the most notorious child murderers and serial killers, including the following 10:
Richard Allen Davis

In 1993, Richard Allen Davis broke into a Petaluma residence and kidnapped 12-year-old Polly Ann Klaas, who had been having a sleepover at her home with two friends. Davis strangled Polly and left her body in a remote area in Cloverdale.
Richard Allen Davis, who is imprisoned at San Quentin State Prison, was sentenced to death for kidnapping Polly Klaas from a sleepover at knifepoint and then strangling her. (Klaas Kids)
In 1996, a Santa Clara County Superior Court judge sentenced Davis to death. His previous crimes helped prompt California’s Three Strikes law.
Polly’s father, Marc Klaas, later founded the nonprofit organization KlassKids Foundation, which operated for 30 years and assisted in the search for millions of missing children.
The Alphabet Killer

Between 1977 and 1994, Joseph Naso killed at least four women in Contra Costa, Marin and Yuba counties. He became known as the "Alphabet Killer" after choosing women who had the same letters in their first and last name.
INDIANA, FLORIDA AND ALABAMA CARRY OUT RARE US TRIPLE EXECUTION DAY
Joseph Naso listens to proceedings during his arraignment in Marin County Superior Court in San Rafael, Calif., April 13, 2011. (MediaNews Group/Marin Independent Journal via Getty Images)
In 2013, a Marin County Superior Court judge sentenced Naso to death.
The Yosemite Serial Killer
In February 1999, Cary Stayner killed four people near Yosemite National Park.
Stayner, a handyman at the nearby Cedar Lodge, murdered Carole Sund, 42. He also murdered and sexually assaulted her daughter Juli, 15, and killed family friend Silvina Pelosso, 16.
Months later, he beheaded a 26-year-old nature guide identified as Joie Armstrong.
MULTIPLE DEATH SENTENCES IN DIFFERENT STATES ARE SET TO BE CARRIED OUT WITHIN 24 HOURS: 'NOT VERY COMMON'

Motel handyman Cary Stayner pictured in a July 29, 1999, mugshot. He was charged Oct. 20, 1999, with capital murder in the killings of three Yosemite sightseers. He was also linked to a fourth slaying. (California Department of Corrections)
In 2002, a Santa Clara County Superior Court judge sentenced Stayner to death for the murders of Sund and the teen girls. He was already serving a life sentence for murdering Armstrong.
Stayner first became notable as the older brother of Steven Stayner, who escaped a 1972 kidnapping in 1980.
'THRILL KILLER' AND DESERT EXECUTIONER — MEET THE DOZENS OF CRIMINALS DEM AG BACKED FOR PAROLE: 'NO BRAINER'
The Southside Slayer
Between 1987 and 1998, Chester Turner raped and murdered low-income women in South Los Angeles, often abandoning their bodies in dark alleys or vacant lots.

Authorities arrested Turner in 2003, after a DNA database matched him to the victims. He became known as the "Southside Slayer" after targeting women in the South Figueroa Street corridor, between Gage Avenue and 108th Street in Los Angeles County.
FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD
Chester Turner appears during the first day of his trial in Los Angeles April 3, 2007. (Anne Cusack/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
In 2007, a Los Angeles County Superior Court judge sentenced Turner to death for killing 10 women. In 2014, he received another death sentence for the killings of four additional women.
Christopher Cheary

In 2011, Christopher Cheary murdered, raped and tortured Sophia Acosta, identified as his girlfriend’s 3-year-old daughter. The incident happened while he babysat Sophia and her sister at an Exeter apartment.

The child’s mother, who was not charged in the case, reported the crime after finding Sophia unconscious with head wounds. Medical staff later testified about finding internal trauma on the victim, including signs of sexual torture.
Christopher Cheary was found guilty of the 2011 murder of 3-year-old Sophia Acosta. (Tulare County District Attorney's Office)
Following a 2016 conviction, a Tulare County Superior Court judge sentenced Cheary to death in 2017.
The Scorecard Killer
Between 1971 and 1983, Randy Kraft raped, tortured and killed at least 16 hitchhikers and young men across Southern California, although authorities believe he murdered over 60 people.

He became known as the "Scorecard Killer" after investigators found a scorecard in his vehicle, listing victims with the locations of bodies written in code. Kraft’s killing spree ended in 1983, when California Highway Patrol officers pulled him over and found deceased Marine Terry Lee Gambrel in his vehicle, in the front passenger seat.

Randy Steven Kraft, pictured at left, in 1983, and at right in June 2007, is likely California's most prolific serial killer. He may have killed as many as 65 young men in Oregon, Michigan and California during a 13-year span that ended in 1983. He was sentenced to die after a trial that lasted nearly a year. His killing spree came to an end when he was stopped on suspicion of drunken driving in 1981 with a dead Marine in his Toyota. (California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation via Getty Images)
Authorities linked 43 victims to coded handwriting on the scorecard but chose to charge Kraft with 16 to narrow the burden of proof.

In 1989, an Orange County Superior Court judge sentenced Kraft to death.
Isauro Aguirre
In 2013, Isauro Aguirre and girlfriend Pearl Fernandez killed 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez after torturing him for eight months in a Palmdale residence.
The torture, in part, included depriving Gabriel of food, beating him, forcing him to eat cat feces and locking him alone in a cabinet with a sock shoved inside his mouth.

Isauro Aguirre appears in Lancaster Superior Court May 28, 2013. He was later convicted and sentenced to death for the torture and murder of his girlfriend's 8-year-old son, Gabriel Fernandez. (Irfan Khan/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

In 2018, a Los Angeles County Superior Court judge sentenced Aguirre to death, while Fernandez received life in prison without parole.

Charles Ng
Between 1983 and 1985, Charles abducted, tortured and murdered at least 11 people. The murders took place at a remote cabin, known as "The Castle" in Calaveras County.

Convicted murderer Charles Ng enters Orange County Superior Court in Santa Ana, where a jury recommended that he be put to death for killing 11 people in Northern California in 1984. (Al Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

The Trailside Killer
Between 1980 and 1981, David Carpenter, also known as the "Trailside Killer," raped and murdered at least seven hikers in Marin County and Santa Cruz.
Public defender Frank Cox, left, at the defense table with David Carpenter, in San Rafael, Calif., in December 1984. (MediaNews Group/Marin Independent Journal via Getty Images)

title: Border Patrol seizes nearly $10M in cocaine during back-to-back California stops
summary: Border Patrol agents found 550 vacuum-sealed packages of suspected cocaine in two vehicles just three minutes apart at the San Clemente checkpoint.
story: Border Patrol agents seized more than 1,435 pounds of suspected cocaine worth $9.8 million during two vehicle inspections just three minutes apart at a Southern California checkpoint.
U.S. Border Patrol agents seized nearly $10 million in cocaine during two vehicle inspections just three minutes apart at a Southern California checkpoint, authorities said.

Agents discovered more than 1,435 pounds of suspected cocaine valued at $9.8 million during inspections at the San Clemente Border Patrol checkpoint last month, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

On Oct. 25, agents assigned to the San Diego Sector referred the two vehicles for additional inspection after observing "suspicious behavior," including one driver attempting to reverse out of the checkpoint.
A Border Patrol canine alerted agents to both vehicles, leading to the discovery of 550 vacuum-sealed packages concealed inside black garbage bags.
CBP OFFICERS SEIZE OVER $2.8M IN COCAINE AND METH IN BACK-TO-BACK BUSTS AT CALIFORNIA PORT OF ENTRY

U.S. Border Patrol agents seized more than 1,435 pounds of suspected cocaine valued at $9.8 million during two vehicle inspections just three minutes apart at a Southern California checkpoint. (U.S. Customs and Border Protection)
Field tests yielded presumptive positive results for cocaine, CBP said.
"With this seizure, we are heading for a record year in narcotics interdictions here at the San Clemente checkpoint," San Clemente Station Patrol Agent in Charge J.D. Scott said in a statement.
"A few years ago, our agents were deployed to the immediate border and processed hundreds of illegal aliens," Scott continued.
"With illegal border entries in San Diego at all-time lows, we now have the agents needed to keep our checkpoint open longer and to maintain a strong Border Patrol presence along our I-5 corridor."
CBP OFFICERS SEIZE $67 MILLION IN ILLEGAL DRUGS AT SAN DIEGO BORDER PORTS, DHS SAYS

Border Patrol agents discovered 550 vacuum-sealed packages of suspected cocaine concealed inside black garbage bags during inspections at the San Clemente checkpoint on Oct. 25, 2026. (U.S. Customs and Border Protection)
Both drivers were arrested, and the Drug Enforcement Administration took custody of the suspects and suspected narcotics pending federal prosecution.
The seizures come amid the Trump administration's broader crackdown on drug cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations and human smuggling and drug trafficking networks.

Authorities discovered 550 vacuum-sealed packages of suspected cocaine hidden in black garbage bags inside two vehicles at a California Border Patrol checkpoint. (U.S. Customs and Border Protection)
In a separate case in May, authorities in the Southern District of California uncovered more than a ton of cocaine worth an estimated $45 million linked to an alleged cross-border drug tunnel.

title: Denver man found dead at bottom of national park canyon beneath steep drop-offs
summary: A drone team located human remains on the floor of Gunnison National Park's Black Canyon after deputies found an abandoned vehicle on the South Rim.
story: John N. Countryman, 57, of Denver, was found dead in Black Canyon after deputies discovered an abandoned vehicle near the Colorado national park.
Colorado authorities on Wednesday said a man was found dead at Gunnison National Park last week after deputies discovered an abandoned vehicle near the park.

The Montrose County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) said the body was found on the floor of the park’s Black Canyon, where many trails run along steep 2,000-foot drop-offs and access to the inner canyon is limited.
The hiker was identified as John N. Countryman, 57, of Denver, officials said in a post on Facebook.
BODY OF MISSING HIKER FOUND IN OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK THANKS TO CRUCIAL CLUE

A creek runs through the Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park July 29, 2020. Authorities identified a Denver man whose body was discovered in a remote section of Black Canyon last week. (RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images/File)
The sheriff's office said deputies were first notified Oct. 27 around 5:30 p.m. of an "abandoned vehicle parked near mile marker 10 along the South Rim of Black Canyon."
Personal belongings were also discovered near Devil's Lookout, one of the park's steepest viewing points.
VIDEO SHOWS HIGH-ALTITUDE RESCUE OF HIKER WHO FELL HUNDREDS OF FEET DOWN UTAH'S MOUNT TIMPANOGOS

Two visitors look out over Black Canyon inside Gunnison National Park from a high viewpoint near the location where the Montrose County Sheriff's Office recovered a body last week. (RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images)
The sheriff's office drone team was then called in to search the canyon for a possible missing person connected to the abandoned vehicle.
However, the team was unable to locate anyone before nightfall due to "diminishing daylight," authorities said.
After a search at approximately 6:30 a.m. the following morning, the drone team "confirmed the presence of human remains on the canyon floor."
Countryman's body was recovered two days later and transferred to the Montrose County Coroner's Office.
The cause and manner of death remain under investigation.

title: Secret Service arrests armed Venezuelan migrant near White House over alleged Trump assassination threat
summary: Secret Service officers arrested a Venezuelan migrant in Washington, D.C., after finding guns in a stolen vehicle and hearing an alleged threat against President Donald Trump.
story: Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos allegedly told Secret Service agents that voices directed him to travel to Washington and kill President Donald Trump.

An illegal immigrant from Venezuela was arrested near the White House Thursday after he was allegedly found inside a stolen vehicle carrying multiple guns and reportedly threatening to kill President Donald Trump, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

U.S. Secret Service officers approached the suspect Thursday evening after spotting him "acting suspicious in his car while it was parked on Constitution Avenue in Washington, D.C.," DHS told Fox News.
The suspect told officers he had heard voices in his head telling him to travel to the nation's capital and kill Trump, DHS said.
Officers subsequently learned that the vehicle had been reported stolen, and the suspect admitted to having weapons inside, according to DHS.
CAR RAMS INTO WHITE HOUSE BARRICADE, SUSPECT ARRESTED: OFFICIALS
The suspect, Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, is an illegal alien from Venezuela. (DHS)
A search of the vehicle reportedly turned up three guns, including an AR-15-style rifle and two handguns, along with dozens of rounds of ammunition.
The suspect was identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, who illegally entered the country through Texas in March 2024 and was subsequently arrested by U.S. Border Patrol, according to officials.
He was later released into the country under the Biden administration, authorities said.
After his arrest, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer for Chrinos with the U.S. Marshals Service, which currently has custody of Chrinos.
The U.S. Secret Service said the incident reflects a growing threat posed by armed individuals "drawn to the White House complex."
Weapons and ammunition were retrieved from the suspect’s car, including an AR-15-style weapon, a Mac 10, and a Glock 43X. (DHS)

"This is the latest example of Secret Service personnel relying on extensive training and experience to de-escalate a volatile situation that posed an imminent threat to our protectees and other Americans," U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said in a statement.
"While our personnel are trained to respond to situations like this, and we remain confident in our tactics, we are alarmed by the increase in threat cases that continue to arise."
To disrupt threats before they arrive in Washington, Curran said the agency will continue to "focus on proactively investigating and identifying individuals" who raise suspicion.
SECRET SERVICE DETAINS, QUESTIONS INDIVIDUAL WHO DROVE VEHICLE INTO BARRICADE NEAR WHITE HOUSE
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin also commended the Secret Service for intervening before the suspect could harm anyone.

"This is just an example of the incredible work done by the men and women of the Secret Service every single day as they put their lives on the line to protect our nation’s leaders," Mullin said in a statement.

Chrinos was charged with carrying a rifle outside a home or business, three counts of unlawful transportation of a firearm, three counts of possessing an unregistered firearm, three counts of possessing unregistered ammunition, possession of certain dangerous weapons, carrying a pistol without a license, unauthorized use of a motor vehicle, theft and receiving stolen property.

U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference. Mullin commended the Secret Service for stopping an armed suspect near the White House Thursday evening.  (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

The latest incident comes amid a series of alarming encounters and security breaches near the nation's capital.

Just three months ago, a California resident was found near Capitol Hill after driving cross-country with an operational 10-foot guillotine in his pickup truck. He was identified as Philan-Tam-Duy Le.
In two separate but similar incidents, suspects also rammed vehicles into security barricades near the White House in March 2026 and October 2025.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: California prosecutors revolt after Newsom orders state's worst killers off death row
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's blanket clemency for 548 death row inmates draws outrage from prosecutors, including in the Gabriel Fernandez case.
story: Decades after his daughter Polly Klaas was murdered, Marc Klaas speaks out against California Gov. Gavin Newsom's potential plan to commute California’s remaining death sentences, calling the move a betrayal of crime victims and voters.

Shortly after California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his plans for clemency for hundreds of death row inmates in the Golden State, current and former prosecutors from across the state issued shocked responses to his push for blanket commutations.

Among those slated to have their frozen death penalties commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole is Isauro Aguirre, the Palmdale man convicted in 2017 of torturing and murdering his girlfriend's 8-year-old son, Gabriel Fernandez, who died in 2013.
"It’s horrible," Jonathan Hatami, the deputy Los Angeles district attorney who prosecuted the case, told Fox News Digital.
'BABY KILLERS, COP KILLERS' HAVE AN ALLY IN NEWSOM, MURDERED GIRL'S FATHER SAYS AMID DEATH ROW CONTROVERSY

Los Angeles 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez died in 2013 after months of horrific abuse from his mother's boyfriend, whose death sentence is expected to be commuted to life without parole in a new push for clemency by California Gov. Gavin Newsom. (Gabriel's Justice/Facebook)
Hatami told Fox News Digital that the governor's decision came without any discussions with Gabriel's family. On X, he reposted his heart-wrenching closing argument from before Aguirre's sentencing.

"Death was likely a merciful end to Gabriel’s pain — and that only illuminates the torture and abuse that he really suffered," Hatami said at the time. "When he needed it most, no one was there to hold Gabriel, to love him, to caress him, and to just tell him ‘everything will be alright.’"
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Aguirre tortured the child for more than seven months before beating him so severely he died with a fractured skull and broken ribs. The abuse included shooting him with a BB gun, burning his genitals and forcing him to eat cat feces. Prosecutors alleged that Aguirre hated the second-grader because he was gay. Gabriel's mother was also sentenced to prison.

Isauro Aguirre appears in Lancaster Superior Court on Tuesday, May 28, 2013. He was later convicted and sentenced to death for the torture and murder of his girlfriend's 8-year-old son, Gabriel Fernandez. (Irfan Khan/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
"The defendant is not a victim," Hatami said in his closing argument. Aguirre, he said, was "pure evil" and a "coward."
NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

Among the prisoners who would benefit from Newsom's decision are the state's worst — those who have tortured their victims, like Aguirre, murdered children, gunned down police and even serial killers.

The "Scorecard Killer," Randy Kraft, killed 16 men between 1972 and 1983. The "Trailside Killer," David Carpenter, killed seven people on hiking trails between 1980 and 1981. "Yosemite Killer," Cary Stayner, murdered a mother, her daughter, the girl's friend and another woman in 1999. Charles Ng was sentenced to death for his role in the abduction and torture, rape and murder of 11 people between 1984 and 1985, including two infants.

"I am not aware of any victims’ family members receiving notice of these commutations from the Governor," San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson said in his own statement, in which he called Newsom's move "the wrong decision."

Handout photo provided by the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation." Randy Steven Kraft, left in 1983, right in June 2007, likely California's most prolific serial killer, may have killed as many as 65 young men in Oregon, Michigan and California during a 13-year span that ended in 1983. He was sentenced to die after a trial that lasted nearly a year. His killing spree came to an end when he was stopped on suspicion of drunken driving in 1981 with a dead Marine in his Toyota. (California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation via Getty Images)
Newsom, however, wrote in an open letter to state residents that the state "cannot morally kill" them.

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," he wrote — later acknowledging that those who would benefit from his move "caused indescribable suffering to victims, their families, communities, and our state as a whole."

Current Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman, along with counterparts in Orange, Sacramento and other counties, have issued statements noting that they will continue to consider the death penalty on future eligible cases following Newsom's surprise announcement Thursday, noting that his action does not change state law or abolish capital punishment.
Public defender Frank Cox, left, at the defense table with David Carpenter, in San Rafael, Calif., in December 1984. (MediaNews Group/Marin Independent Journal via Getty Images)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"Every death sentence results from years of legal proceedings, involving juries, judges, and multiple layers of mandatory appellate review," Sacramento District Attorney Thien Ho noted in a statement. "A blanket commutation of all death sentences disregards the individualized facts and circumstances of each case, the careful judicial process that led to those lawful sentences, and the voices of victims who have waited decades for justice."
While California hasn't executed a condemned inmate in 20 years, death row inmates have largely been excluded from progressive criminal justice reforms made to lighten sentences on other offenders.

Convicted murderer Charles Ng enters the Orange County Superior Court in Santa Ana, where a jury recommended that he be put to death for killing 11 people in Northern California in 1984. (Al Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON

"Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutation of the death sentences of all 548 condemned inmates in California is mercy for the wolves...while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep," Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer said in a statement.

With death row off the table, critics like Spitzer consider them closer to further leniency.
Governor Gavin Newsom appears at the California Economic Summit in Long Beach, California, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images)

title: Florida Learjet crash investigators dig up engine piece after pilots warned of rough weather ahead
summary: NTSB crews recovered part of an engine from the Learjet 60 crash site in Greenacres, Florida, as the probe focuses on icing and turbulence reports.
story: Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley discusses the aircraft's damaged tail components, rapid descent and encounter with severe weather, as investigators work to determine what caused the deadly Florida Learjet crash.
Federal investigators have recovered part of an engine from the Learjet that slammed into the ground Sunday in Greenacres, Florida, killing all nine people aboard.

Crews started excavating the site Wednesday, once utility workers had drained water and cleared other hazards, the National Transportation Safety Board said Thursday. The Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport around 10:37 a.m. Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. Just before 1 p.m., it plunged into Palm Beach County, killing everyone aboard.
Once digging began, investigators uncovered a portion of one engine, officials said, noting that debris had also turned up on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings.
Earlier in the week, investigators recovered the left tail elevator, which controls the jet's pitch, in three separate pieces, one of them nearly four miles from where the Learjet 60 went down.
PRIVATE JET WITH 9 PEOPLE ON BOARD CRASHES JUST MILES FROM MAR-A-LAGO

Adam Robinson and his wife, Helen Sharp, were traveling with their two young children when the Learjet carrying them from Texas to the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Nov. 1. (Fox News)
National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas B. Chapman called the part a "very important piece of evidence" when he spoke to reporters Tuesday.
"Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened," the agency wrote on social media.

A Learjet 60 slammed into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday afternoon, erupting into a massive fireball just nine miles from Mar-a-Lago. (Aki Kuusisto via Storyful)

INVESTIGATORS ZERO IN ON POSSIBLE CAUSE OF WISCONSIN PLANE CRASH THAT KILLED 6
A map shows the Learjet’s flight from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas toward the Bahamas before it crashed in Greenacres, Florida. (Fox News)

title: Ex-MIT professor wins $6M after sex claims wrecked career, accuser joked about ‘#hetoo’
summary: David Sabatini's $6 million defamation win over Kristin Knouse now faces cross-appeals as both sides prepare to battle in Massachusetts courts.
story: Former MIT biologist David Sabatini won a $6 million defamation verdict against Kristin Knouse over sexual misconduct claims. Both sides now prepare cross-appeals.

A Massachusetts jury awarded former MIT biologist Dr. David Sabatini a $6 million defamation victory over sexual misconduct claims, setting the stage for cross-appeals as both legal teams prepare to take the case to a higher court.

Dr. Kristin Knouse, the former colleague whose sexual misconduct allegations dismantled Sabatini's American academic career, is challenging the October verdict. Her decision triggered a battle over legal consequences surrounding workplace misconduct claims and the authority of campus tribunals.

Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zucker, believes that the $6 million verdict could potentially stop female scientists from reporting misconduct, claiming the jury's decision reflects a society that refuses to believe women who challenge powerful men.
David Sabatini listens to closing arguments in a pair of lawsuits on Oct. 14, 2026. (David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD WINS LEGAL BATTLE AFTER VOLLEYBALL COACH'S $250M DEFAMATION SUIT IS DISMISSED

"When someone can get sued for having spoken out, that kills the willingness of anyone to participate in an investigation," Zucker told Fox News Digital. "Daring to speak out will get you sued, [and] the likelihood that anyone would come forward goes down a lot."
Sabatini’s legal team rejected the narrative. His attorney, Lisa G. Arrowood, told Fox News Digital that the verdict poses zero threat to genuine victims.
"The jury verdict in this case should have no impact on women who truly have been harassed or abused and decide to report the misconduct," Arrowood said.

"What the jury found here, based on the contemporaneous documents written by Dr. Knouse herself, was that no harassment ever occurred and that her claims of harassment and rape were false and defamatory. This jury verdict, therefore, has no bearing on people who report truthfully."
The Maclaurin Buildings on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on Tuesday, Dec. 12, 2023. (Getty Images)
Arrowood also expressed confidence that the $6 million penalty would withstand appeal.
"This is her right," Arrowood said. "However, the judge was very careful in this case and frequently ruled in her favor on many close calls. We think her appeal will be unsuccessful."
FORMER CAL SOFTBALL PLAYER FILES LAWSUIT AGAINST UNIVERSITY, FEMALE EX-COACH OVER ALLEGED SEXUAL MISCONDUCT
Zucker argued that the verdicts will not stand, warning that penalizing accusers threatens future institutional investigations.

"We do not believe the verdicts will stand," Zucker said. "Our client came to court and told the truth about her experiences with Sabatini, as did multiple other women; investigators uncovered several violations of institutional policy."
The upcoming appellate fight will scrutinize the events that led to the lawsuit.
Consensual or coerced

The pair first met in 2012, when Knouse was a doctoral student in the Harvard-MIT M.D./Ph.D. program and Sabatini served on her thesis committee. By 2018 — after Knouse had been named a Whitehead Fellow — they began a relationship, according to court documents.
FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL

Sabatini maintained the relationship was consensual. Knouse alleged it was coerced and that Sabatini created an inappropriate workplace dynamic. A 2021 Whitehead investigation found Sabatini violated its workplace relationship policy.
Text messages made public during the case showed Knouse wrote that she would "fixate on how I’m being held as a backup and competed against other women," Boston 25 News reported.
In one message about visiting Sabatini's hotel room one night on a work retreat, she wrote: "In hindsight, it was quite aggressive, #hetoo," according to the outlet.
Knouse launched a campaign against Sabatini that she called "Covert Operation Dethrone," Boston 25 reported, and joked in one message about buying a "Lambo" if she won a settlement.

Kristin Knouse, left, sits behind the bar with Lexi Foman, assistant to retired Judge Nancy Gertner. A motions hearing, in the cases of David Sabatini vs. Whitehead Institute and Kristin Knouse and Knouse vs. Sabatini, is held in Suffolk Superior Court in front of Judge Hélène Kazanjian. (Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

"Dr. Sabatini and his legal team do not criticize the MeToo movement or the right of women to complain of harassment," Arrowood added. "This case is unique in that the jury found that Dr. Knouse’s claims were fabricated and designed to cause harm to Dr. Sabatini."

After Knouse accused him of sexual misconduct, MIT administrators stripped Sabatini of his tenured position. The Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) dismissed him. The Whitehead Institute ousted him.
CBS NEWS FACES $20M DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AFTER MISIDENTIFYING MARYLAND TEENAGER IN REFLECTING POOL REPORT
Arrowood said that Sabatini’s team is launching its own counter-offensive on appeal, seeking to overturn the court’s earlier decision that dismissed the Whitehead Institute from the lawsuit.
MIT and HHMI were not defendants in the defamation lawsuit.

MIT declined to comment but referred Fox News Digital to a letter sent out to staff in 2022, when Sabatini resigned and the school said he was found to have "behaved in ways incompatible with the responsibilities of faculty membership."
HHMI did not respond to a request for comment.
BIDEN OFFICIALS CIRCUMVENTED COURT ORDER IN TITLE IX CASES, INCLUDING MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS, DOCS SHOW
Title IX Investigations

The universities based their firings on internal Title IX investigations, which concluded that Sabatini violated policies by entering into an undisclosed romantic relationship with a junior researcher.
The campus tribunals require a low burden of proof, which rarely allows the accused to cross-examine the accuser, according to the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression.
Arrowood argued that the institutions rushed to judgment before the facts could be tested in a civil court.
"This verdict should send universities the message that all the facts and documents from both sides need to be obtained and analyzed before deciding to fire someone," she said.
SEND US A TIP

"Here, the investigators and the Whitehead Institute allowed one party and her lawyers to control what evidence they received and even what they could show to Dr. Sabatini. Had the full picture been shown to the institution and to the investigators, we believe the outcome would have been different."

Former MIT scientist David Sabatini, a biologist who once generated Nobel Prize buzz, is hoping for a comeback after he was abruptly ousted amid allegations of sexual harassment. (Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
GOT A TIP?
When the legal battle reached a Suffolk County courtroom, the jury denied Knouse’s counterclaims of harassment and instead ordered her to pay Sabatini millions for defamation.

While Sabatini won the courtroom battle, the years-long ordeal destroyed his U.S. research operation. Activist billionaire Bill Ackman stepped in and funded a new laboratory for Sabatini in Prague, where Sabatini continues his life-saving cancer research.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"I lost everything. There was nothing left of my normal life," Sabatini previously told Boston 25 News. "I've been dreaming about this moment for all this time, but often thinking I might not make it, financially, emotionally or physically."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The case now moves to the Massachusetts appellate courts. The formal briefing schedule is pending.

title: Clash in the castle: Medieval Times dinner theater insiders allege animal cruelty, sexual harassment
summary: A former Medieval Times Dinner & Tournament queen alleges sexual harassment, cyberbullying and doxxing in a lawsuit targeting workplace culture.
story: Medieval Times faces lawsuits alleging animal cruelty, sexual harassment, gender discrimination, bullying, doxxing and retaliation from former employees at its castles.
For 43 years, Medieval Times Dinner & Tournament performers across North America have captivated audiences as jousting knights and bejeweled ladies on horseback.

But now the company’s own castle is under siege as former employees allege in lawsuits that the company shrouds a culture of animal cruelty, sexual harassment, discrimination, bullying and retaliation for reporting abuse.
At the shows, guests dine on what’s billed as a medieval-style feast, as they cheer on armor-clad knights, who participate in a tournament on horseback and battle with swords.
The chain established its first location in Kissimmee, Florida, near Orlando, in 1983. The company now employs more than 2,000 at 10 "castles" in the United States and Canada.

William Elliot III, 35, assistant head knight and former magician in Las Vegas, makes the grand entrance as the red knight, along with fellow knights during a show at Medieval Times in Buena Park on Friday, June 28, 2013. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
MEDIEVAL-THEMED LIVE SHOWS DRAW YOUNG WOMEN WHO ARE LOOKING FOR LOVE AND JADED BY MODERN DATING: REPORT
The theater’s show champions the "chivalry" of their knights. But some who work alongside those performers say the culture is biased against female cast members.
A former "queen" of the castle is now suing the company, alleging a workplace environment "rooted in gender discrimination and sexual harassment."
Another whistleblower alleged that she was fired for voicing concerns about animal cruelty.
FORMER DISNEY CHANNEL STAR ALLEGES SHE WAS SEXUALLY ABUSED AT 14 AFTER BEING TOLD TO ‘BOND’ WITH EMPLOYEE
Royal rivalry
A civil lawsuit was filed in June by a former cast member of the Buena Park, California, castle. She alleges a hostile work environment with widespread sexual harassment.

Kaitlyn Farrell resigned in February 2024 because of "intolerable" conditions after joining the company as a "queen" five years earlier, according to the lawsuit filed in the Superior Court of California, in Orange County.
The "two-tiered workplace culture" treats female cast members as "a lesser class of employee," she said in the lawsuit.
Farrell alleges that unwanted sexual advances toward female employees are "normalized" and "gender-based misconduct" and that complaints are "dismissed" with "indifference."
While working at Medieval Times, she was asked to be a witness in a workplace harassment investigation for another employee.
That made her the "target of open retaliation by the very employee she reported on," her lawsuit alleges.
Management stood by and did nothing, she said.

On another occasion, according to the lawsuit, a manager ordered someone to "remove stitching" from her costumes, what she calls a "calculated sabotage" that was "maliciously intended to cause wardrobe malfunctions in front of live audiences."

After employees unionized at the Buena Park location, and she participated in a strike in February 2023, Farrell said she became the "primary target of an extreme, sexualized cyberbullying and doxxing campaign."

Brandon Sanchez, who plays a knight, protests outside Medieval Times in Buena Park, California, on Wednesday, March 8, 2023. Performers picketed the Buena Park castle after launching an unfair labor practice strike against management. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)

Anonymous social media accounts with "obvious indications" of employee or management involvement posted content such as her dating history, sexually derogatory captions and photoshopped images with her face "on the bodies of semi-nude cartoon characters depicted in simulated sexual positions," the lawsuit alleges.
DISNEYLAND, ACTORS' UNION CLASH OVER PARENTAL LEAVE, BENEFITS AS UNION NEGOTIATES FIRST CONTRACT

The harassment escalated to physical stalking when Medieval Times employees "traveled to Ms. Farrell's secondary workplace" at another theme park "to physically intimidate her while she was working" to entertain guests, the lawsuit alleges.
When she made formal complaints about the behavior, an attorney for Medieval Times issued a written letter dismissing the cyberbullying and stalking as "weird allegations."
"We look forward to proving these allegations in court," Farrell’s attorney, Charles Ludd Jr., told Fox News Digital.
‘False claims’
Medieval Times did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. But former employee Bill Elliot calls Farrell’s allegations "false claims."
Elliot worked at the same Medieval Times location as a knight until leaving after 12 1/2 years in 2015. He had no complaints with the company, he told Fox News Digital in a text message.
"The company took care of us," he said. "We had decent pay; full-time hours with overtime … full medical, dental and vision insurance; and 401K."

William Elliot III, 35, assistant head knight and former magician in Las Vegas, prepares to throw a flower to an audience member as he performs as the red knight during a show at Medieval Times in Buena Park on Friday, June 28, 2013. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
He believes that people making claims against the company are part of "the-rich-need-to-pay-their-fair-share group" and want to cash in, he said.
"They have no responsibility in running a company that employs thousands of people and no risk in doing it, but believe they deserve more of the profit," he said.
"If it was such a toxic environment and company, they could have immediately removed themselves, but didn't," he said.
It was common for female cast members to seek "attention from the knights and [they] did everything to try and get that attention," Elliot said.
"Now, because those females didn't get their way or what they wanted, they started making false claims and screaming ‘toxic masculinity’ or any other buzzwords to get attention."
Animal-cruelty allegations
Farrell’s lawsuit isn’t the first to make concerning claims against the dinner theater company.

In her 2019 lawsuit, Bethany Regan tells about how she joined the Buena Park castle in 2013. During her employment, she was treated "less favorably" than male cast members, according to court documents.
When she became increasingly concerned about the welfare of the equine performers, she made reports to management, the lawsuit alleges.
The head trainer had a "volatile temper" and would whip horses "unnecessarily" until they had "large welts" over their body, according to the lawsuit.

Some horses were trained in ways that made them bleed from their mouths and in various places on their bodies, she alleged. Horses were "overworked" and sometimes weren’t allowed to rest until they were dehydrated, according to her complaint.
One horse died as a result, she alleged.
Regan had been warned that the head horse trainer was a close friend of the owner of the company and that any complaints could result in "retaliation." She brought up her concerns anyway.
She also reported "dangerous and unsafe working conditions" for female cast members.
After she made formal complaints, the company suspended her for "starting rumors," her lawsuit alleges. Later, her job was terminated.
The lawsuit was settled in 2020. The conditions of the settlement were not made public.
Regan’s attorney did not respond to a request from Fox News Digital for comment.
Horses in the spotlight

Yvonne Barteau was principal trainer and director of entertainment operations for six years at Arabian Nights Dinner Attraction. Minutes away from a Florida Medieval Times castle, the horse-themed dinner theater operated from 1988 until 2014.
Barteau now runs a horse rescue in Florida called Horses without Humans. She founded the operation after making a documentary about theater horses in the United States.
Over the years, she worked with many Medieval Times performers as they moved between dinner theater jobs in the Orlando, Florida, area, she told Fox News Digital.
It was common for young performers to get "way too into their role, like they're really medieval warriors," Barteau said. "I think they got too into the identity."
Yvonne Barteau performs with her grey stallion, Papi, at Spirit of the Horse. (Courtesy of Cheri Prill/Stunning Steeds Photography)
That led to men treating women in a "callous" way, she said, "and I think it was not frowned upon the way that it should be. So yeah, certainly back then, I saw it."
Dinner theater jobs "seemed to attract people like that. And then sometimes the upper management didn't shut it down like they should have," she said.
She met "good people" at Medieval Times. She met others that were not so good, she said.
And there’s never an excuse for abusing a horse, she said.
"Anybody that works with horses, or works with something that has no voice of its own—children, horses, any animal—you have to be the voice," she said.
But "in today’s culture," she said, people with little experience with horses assume that any performance with a horse should be considered cruel.
SEND US A TIP
And that’s simply wrong, she said.
GOT A TIP?
"They haven't seen how some horses really do light up, and they do love to be out there performing," she said. "They love the attention."
She has performed for years with a stallion named Papi.

"He's an absolute theater horse—he's a Brad Pitt.

"People see that horse, and they remember him, and it makes them love horses. And why wouldn't we want that, you know, as horse lovers? Why would we want somebody else to fall in love with horses?"

title: Police identify agent killed after suspect opens fire near Colorado bus, wounds other 3 officers
summary: A suspect trying to board an RTD bus near Denver opened fire on Lakewood police officers, killing one and wounding three others Thursday evening.
story: One Colorado police agent was killed in a shooting in Lakewood on Thursday night, while three other agents were wounded, according to officials.
The police officer who was fatally shot Thursday evening after officers approached a suspect boarding a bus outside Denver has been identified as 33-year-old Nicholas Allen Graham.

"The Lakewood Police Department is devastated to announce that the fourth agent, 33-year-old Agent Nicholas Graham, died as a result of being shot by the suspect," the city of Lakewood said in an updated news release.

During a press conference Friday, Police Chief Philip Smith described Graham as an excellent agent who served on the department's major crimes team, where he handled "some of our community's most serious crimes, including homicide, domestic violence, and stalking."
In 2023, Graham received the Special Investigations Unit Wingman Award for his gang intelligence work, investigative support and assistance with major SWAT cases, Smith said.
Graham reportedly joined the Lakewood Police Department in early 2019, where he worked alongside members of his family.
"Nick was part of a police family. His father's recently retired. His mother worked in the crime lab," Smith said.
Nicholas Graham, a Lakewood police officer, was killed in a shooting near Denver after a suspect opened fire as officers approached a bus. (City of Lakewood, Colorado)
FOUR DEAD, INCLUDING WASHINGTON DEPUTY, FOLLOWING DOMESTIC CALL SHOOTING; ANOTHER DEPUTY ON LIFE SUPPORT

On Thursday, Lakewood police responded to a report of a suspicious person near the intersection of Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard around 6:30 p.m., where they encountered a suspect attempting to board a bus.
The suspect opened fire on officers, striking four of them, Lakewood Police Public Information Officer John Romero said during a news conference.
"We are very sorry to report that one of those agents has been pronounced dead of their injuries," Romero previously said.
The suspect was shot by police and pronounced dead at the scene, Romero said.
Lakewood Police Public Information Officer John Romero confirmed that one officer was killed, and three others were wounded during a gunfight with a suspect Thursday evening. (KDVR)
A civilian was also injured and transported to a local hospital.
Police did not immediately provide details about the extent of the injuries or the conditions of the three surviving officers.
Authorities said the suspect was attempting to board a Regional Transportation District (RTD) bus when officers approached.
CHICAGO HOSPITAL SHOOTING LEAVES 1 OFFICER DEAD, OTHER 'FIGHTING FOR HIS LIFE'; SUSPECT IN CUSTODY
A Lakewood police agent has died after a shooting Thursday evening and three others were injured. (KDVR)
"Within seconds of agents approaching the suspect, the suspect opened fire on our agents," Romero said.
Romero also delivered an emotional message to the fallen officer's family:
"We just want the family to know that we love them, that we're here for them, and Lakewood Police Department is a family, and we will be here for each other."
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis released a statement following the deadly shooting.
"Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety everyday and I am heartbroken to learn that a Lakewood Police Agent was killed in the line of duty this evening," Polis wrote.

"My heart goes out to their family and friends," he continued. "My thoughts are also with the three agents who are still receiving care at area hospitals, as well as the civilian who was wounded, and I wish them a full and speedy recovery. Thank you to law enforcement who run into danger to keep us safe and to protect our communities."
Polis said the Colorado State Patrol was assisting at the scene and participating in a procession from the hospital honoring the fallen officer.
The Jefferson County Critical Incident Response Team is leading the investigation into the officer-involved shooting, with support from the Colorado Bureau of Investigation.
RTD also released a statement saying it was "deeply concerned" by the shooting.

Lakewood police responded to a report of a suspicious person near Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard around 6:30 p.m. Thursday before a gunfight erupted. (KDVR)
"Our thoughts are with those affected directly by this incident," the statement read. "The safety and well-being of our customers, employees, and partners remain our highest priority."
